2288855.title: Government Strengthens Domestic Fertilizer Production and Supply Chain to Enhance Fertilizer Security
2288855.ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers : Department of Fertilizers
2288855.body_html:
Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :
Department of Fertilizers
Government Strengthens Domestic Fertilizer Production and Supply Chain to Enhance Fertilizer Security
Six New Urea Plants Add 76.2 LMTPA Capacity; Indigenous Urea Production Capacity Rises to 269.42 LMTPA
Strategic Reforms, Capacity Expansion and Global Sourcing Ensure Uninterrupted Fertilizer Availability
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:59PM by PIB Delhi

The Government of India has undertaken a series of strategic initiatives to strengthen domestic fertilizer production, diversify raw material and fertilizer import sources, and ensure uninterrupted availability of fertilizers to farmers despite global supply disruptions and volatility in international markets. According to information received from fertilizer units, fluctuations in fertilizer production are generally influenced by the availability of raw materials and feedstocks, volatility in international prices, and technical shutdowns. To address these challenges, the Government has diversified sources of raw materials and feedstocks to maintain optimum domestic production.

To further strengthen fertilizer supply chains, the Department of Fertilizers has diversified import sources and actively engaged Indian Missions to identify additional suppliers. As a result, 25 Lakh Metric Tonnes (LMT) and 17.7 LMT of urea were secured through global tenders in April 2026 and June 2026, respectively. These initiatives have reduced vulnerabilities arising from global market disruptions and ensured continued fertilizer availability across the country.

Also, following measures are taken by the Government every season for ensuring timely, adequate and uninterrupted supply of fertilizers in the country:

  • Before the commencement of each cropping season, Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with all the State Governments, assesses the State-wise & month-wise requirement of fertilizers.
  • On the basis of requirement projected by DA&FW, D/o Fertilizers allocates adequate quantities of fertilizers to States by issuing monthly supply plan and continuously monitors the availability.
  • The movement of all major subsidized fertilizers is monitored throughout the country by an on-line web-based monitoring system called integrated Fertilizer Management System (iFMS).
  • Regular Weekly Video Conference is conducted jointly by DA&FW and D/o Fertilizers with State Agriculture Officials and corrective actions are taken to dispatch fertilizers as indicated by the State Governments.
  • The distribution of fertilizers within the State is done by the respective State Government.

With regard to Urea, the Government had announced New Investment Policy (NIP) – 2012 on 2nd January, 2013 and its amendment on 7th October, 2014 to facilitate fresh investment in the urea sector and to make India self-sufficient in the urea sector. Total 6 new urea units have been set up under NIP-2012 which includes 4 urea units set up through Joint Venture Companies (JVC) of nominated PSUs and 2 urea units set up by the private companies. The units set up through JVC are Ramagundam urea unit of Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd (RFCL) in Telangana and 3 urea units namely Gorakhpur, Sindri and Barauni of Hindustan Urvarak & Rasayan Limited (HURL) in Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Bihar, respectively. The units set up by private companies are Panagarh urea unit of Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. (Matix) in West Bengal; and Gadepan-III urea unit of Chambal Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. (CFCL) in Rajasthan. Each of these units has installed capacity of 12.7 Lakh Metric Tonne per annum (LMTPA). These units are highly energy efficient as they are based on latest technology. Therefore, these units have together added urea production capacity of 76.2 LMTPA, thereby total indigenous urea production capacity (Reassessed Capacity, RAC) has increased from 207.54 LMTPA during 2014-15 to 269.42 LMTPA during 2026-27. Further, an exclusive policy for the revival of Talcher unit of FCIL through JVC of nominated PSUs namely Talcher Fertilizers Limited (TFL) by setting up a new Greenfield Urea plant of 12.7 LMTPA at coal gasification route has also been approved. Further, setting up of a new Brownfield Ammonia-Urea Complex named as Assam Valley Fertilizer and Chemical Company Ltd. (AVFCCL) with an annual capacity of 12.7 Lakh Metric Tonne of Urea through Joint Venture within the existing premises of Brahmaputra Valley Fertilizer Corporation Limited (BVFCL), Assam has been approved. These two projects are under execution phase.

Also, the Government also notified the New Urea Policy (NUP) – 2015 on 25th May, 2015 for the existing 25 gas-based urea units with one of the objectives of maximizing indigenous urea production beyond RAC. The NUP-2015 has led to additional production of urea by 20-25 LMT as compared to the production during 2014-15 annually.

Above steps together have facilitated increase of Urea production from level of 225 LMT per annum during 2014-15 to a record Urea Production at 314.07 LMT during 2023-24. During 2025-26, 293.30 LMT of Urea was produced in the country.

In addition to this, on 15.07.2026, CCEA approved National Investment Policy for Urea-2026 for Aatmanirbhar Bharat (NIPU-2026) for making fresh investments in Urea Sector.

The Government has implemented Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) Scheme w.e.f. 01.04.2010 for Phosphatic and Potassic (P&K) Fertilizers. Under the Scheme, P&K fertilizers are covered under Open General License (OGL) and companies are free to import/manufacture these fertilizers as per their business dynamics. For Kharif-2026, NBS rates have been approved for Rs. 41,533.81 Cr to ensure availability of P&K fertilizers under the scheme.

To reduce dependence on imported Phosphatic fertilizers and make country self-reliant measures have been taken to encourage domestic production through guidelines 18.01.2024 on reasonableness of MRP, wherein importers/ manufacturers and integrated manufacturers are given reasonable profit of 8%/10% and 12% respectively; based on the requests, the new manufacturing units or increase in manufacturing capacity of existing units have been recognized / taken on record under the NBS Scheme; the number of P&K fertilizers covered under NBS Scheme has increased from 22 grades in 2021 to 28 grades; Freight Subsidy on SSP, which is an indigenously manufactured fertilizer, is being provided since Kharif, 2022 to promote SSP usage for providing Phosphatic or 'P' nutrient to the soil.

This information was provided by Hon’ble Minister of Chemicals & Fertilizers Shri Jagat Prakash Nadda, in a written reply to a question in the Lok Sabha today.

2288853.title: DPIIT's One District One Product Initiative Promotes 1,244 Unique Products Across 773 Districts
2288853.body_html:
Ministry of Commerce & Industry
DPIIT's One District One Product Initiative Promotes 1,244 Unique Products Across 773 Districts
PM Ekta Malls and PMFME Scheme Strengthen Market Access for ODOP Products
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:58PM by PIB Delhi

One District One Product (ODOP) is an initiative by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) with the aim of selecting, branding, and promoting at least one product from each district of the country to enable holistic growth across all regions. The selection of ODOP products is undertaken by the respective State/UT Governments. As of date, 1,244 products have been identified across 773 districts in the country under the ODOP framework.

Several steps have been undertaken to promote and enhance the visibility of the ODOP products includes facilitating participation in domestic and international exhibitions, capacity building initiatives in collaboration with various agencies; e-commerce onboarding drives for Government e-Marketplace (GeM) - ODOP Bazaar.

Under the Scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI), financial assistance of up to ₹200 crore per State/ Union Territories with legislatures - Delhi, Jammu & Kashmir, and Puducherry is provided through a 50-year interest-free loan for establishment of PM Ekta Malls (Unity Malls) to promote the sale of ODOP, GI, and local handicraft products.

The Pradhan Mantri Formalisation of Micro food processing Enterprises (PMFME) Scheme implemented by the Ministry of Food Processing Industries (MoFPI) adopts ODOP approach in food processing sector. It provides 35% credit-linked capital subsidy with maximum for ₹10 lakhs for eligible projects, Seed Capital support to SHG members, Capacity Building through Entrepreneurship Development Programme (EDP) and product-specific training, assistance for Common Infrastructure and Common Incubation Centres, and Branding & Marketing support, including common branding, packaging, quality standardisation and food safety compliance for all the products including ODOP. PMFME Scheme provides support under the Branding & Marketing component @ 50% grant for common branding, packaging, quality standardisation and food safety compliance.

No district-specific financial allocation is made under the ODOP initiative. States/UTs are encouraged to leverage the benefits available under various Central and State Government schemes for the development of ODOP products. These include schemes relating to MSMEs, food processing, skill development, exports, handicrafts, handloom, agriculture, and allied sectors, which provide support for infrastructure development, credit, skill upgradation, quality improvement, branding, market access, and exports.

The PMFME Scheme promotes convergence with other Central initiatives to strengthen both backward and forward linkages. For backward linkages, the Ministry works with the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers' Welfare to facilitate clustering of Farmers with food processing clusters. For forward linkages, Convergence Committees have been constituted with APEDA and the Department of Fisheries to promote export-oriented value chains. Under this convergence, 24 common ODOP product clusters have been identified with APEDA and 7 fish and marine product clusters with MPEDA, to facilitate branding, market access and export promotion.

Under the ‘Districts as Export Hubs’ initiative, the Government aims to promote grassroots export growth by identifying potential products and services across districts in consultation with all stakeholders, including States/UTs. Through this framework, export-potential products and services have been identified in 734 districts. Further, State Export Promotion Committees (SEPCs) and District Export Promotion Committees (DEPCs) has been established across all 36 States/UTs to facilitate implementation and resolve supply chain bottlenecks and 249 District Export Action Plans (DEAPs) have been adopted by their respective DEPCs to streamline the value chain from production to export.

To facilitate market access for ODOP products, a dedicated ODOP Storefront has been established on the Government e-Marketplace (GeM). More than 500 ODOP product categories covering over 1,300 products are available on GeM for procurement. In addition, more than 10 States have developed dedicated e-commerce platforms for marketing and sale of ODOP products. ODOP products are featured at national exhibitions, trade fairs and other promotional events, helping artisans showcase goods and connect with buyers.

For promoting ODOP at international level, collaborated with MEA and Indian Missions abroad to organize promotional events, including exhibitions, buyer–seller meets, and participated in international exhibitions. ODOP Walls have been setup at Indian Missions to showcase ODOP products from various States/Districts. Three international retail stores (two in Singapore and one in Kuwait) are selling ODOP Products. ODOP products have also been included as official gifts during various bilateral/multilateral meetings, thereby enhancing their visibility in international markets.

The initiatives under ODOP have contributed to promotion of local products, improving market access, encouraging entrepreneurship and supporting employment generation. Specific details regarding exports under ODOP is not maintained centrally.

This information was given by Minister of State for Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Shri Jitin Prasada in a written reply in Rajya Sabha today.

2288854.title: 386 Private FM Radio Channels Operational; Govt Policy Mandates 20% Content in Local Language to Promote Regional Culture
2288854.body_html:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
386 Private FM Radio Channels Operational; Govt Policy Mandates 20% Content in Local Language to Promote Regional Culture
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:58PM by PIB Delhi

The Government conducted e-auctions for 730 FM channels across 234 new cities on July 9– 10, 2025 through a transparent system. It was widely published in print and electronic media before the auction. During this cycle, there were 18 successful bidders including 9 new entrants to the FM radio sector. There are 386 operational private FM radio channels.

Under the Private FM Radio policy, every broadcaster must ensure that at least 20% of its daily broadcast content is in the local language of the city and promotes local content, including programmes on local culture, traditions, and folk music.

The Private FM Radio Phase-III policy permits broadcasters to access Prasar Bharati towers and sites, wherever available, for faster rollout. The Government issues Letters of Intent (LOI) and executes Grant of Permission Agreements (GOPA) with clearly defined timelines for operationalisation especially in LWE and aspirational districts.

The Government follows a multi-pronged approach by tracking the broadcast of public service announcements and government schemes. It maintains close coordination with broadcasters for timely dissemination of verified information during emergencies and key campaigns.

This information was provided by the Minister of State for Information and Broadcasting and Parliamentary Affairs, Dr. L. Murugan, in a written reply to an Unstarred Question in the Rajya Sabha raised by Shri I. S. Inbadurai.

2288852.title: Update on Expenditure on Health Research
2288852.ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
2288852.body_html:
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Update on Expenditure on Health Research
Budgetary Allocation for DHR Increases Over Fivefold Since 2014–15, Reaches ₹4,821.21 Crore in 2026–27
24% Increase in DHR Budget Allocation for 2026–27 Underscores Government's Commitment to Strengthening Health Research
Government Expanded Health Research Funding Framework with Enhanced ICMR Grant Architecture
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:56PM by PIB Delhi

The allocation of Department of Health Research (DHR) is 0.012% of GDP. However, in recent years Government has increased the budget in health research along with new programmes/initiatives to make research grants more competitive and accessible. The budgetary allocation for DHR has increased over 5 times - from ₹ 932.00 crores in 2014-15 (RE) to ₹ 4,821.21 in 2026–27 (BE). There has been rise of approximately 24 percent in Budgetary allocation in 2026-27 over the Revised Estimates for 2025–26 (₹3,900.69 crore) indicating strong commitment of Union Government towards strengthening health research in the country.

Government has undertaken measures to broaden and strengthen the health-research funding ecosystem. Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has rationalised and expanded its intramural and extramural grant architecture so that funding support is calibrated to the scale, maturity, risk and translational stage of a research proposal. ICMR has initiated new follow up grants to utilize the leads from the initial research grants. Details are regularly published at ICMR ePMS portal.

The current structure includes Small or ANVESHAN Grants of up to ₹2 crore, Intermediate or NISCHAYAK ANVESHAN Grants ranging from ₹2 crore to ₹8 crore, the First-in-the-World Challenge with stage-linked support of up to ₹8 crore, and Centres for Advanced Research with support of up to ₹15 crore. These instruments support investigator-initiated research, proof-of-concept studies, validation of interventions, high-risk and high-reward innovation, multidisciplinary research and advanced research programmes.

The Union Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare, Shri. Prataprao Jadhav stated this in a written reply in the Lok Sabha today.

Government Expands Global Market Access for Indian Service Providers Through FTAs and Trade Promotion Initiatives
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:55PM by PIB Delhi

In order to enhance services exports, Government of India follows a multi-pronged strategy. It comprises the following:

    1. Focused strategies for enhancing exports are undertaken for specific markets and sectors.
    1. Domestic sectoral challenges impeding services exports are identified in consultation with the stakeholders and addressed through concerned departments/ ministries.
    1. Through Free Trade Agreements
      • Government has secured comprehensive market access and national treatment in services to allow Indian service providers to provide services in key sectors on no less favourable terms through different modes such as cross-border (including digital mode), commercial presence in the FTA partner country and temporary movement of professionals to the partner country. India’s recent FTAs have incorporated disciplines on domestic regulation to ensure that authorisation processes for key services are time-bound, predictable, objective, impartial, and transparent. This ensures that Indian service suppliers do not face challenges in partner countries due to opaque, unpredictable or burdensome regulatory procedures. Through FTAs, India has been able to obtain structured, expedited routes that will facilitate temporary mobility of skilled Indian professionals to provide services in foreign markets.
      • Facilitative provisions for time-bound negotiations of Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) between relevant professional bodies, to facilitate recognition of qualifications and associated licensing requirements. Such MRAs aim to ensure that partner nations accept each other's certifications, and professionals do not have to go through duplicative local testing, additional training, or lengthy re-certification processes before they can practice.

· Some other beneficial provisions are highlighted below :-

        • India has secured supportive framework for Students in FTAs with Australia and New Zealand.
        • Supportive framework related to Social Security Agreements (SSA) to avoid double payments and ensure continuity of social security protection have been secured in recent FTAs such as India-Oman CEPA, the side letter on SSA provisions in India-New Zealand FTA, Double Contribution Convention in India-UK CETA, and in India-EU FTA. Based on the understanding arrived under the India- UK CETA, an agreement on Social Security Contributions was signed on Feb. 10, 2026. This Agreement will ensure that workers will not be required to pay double contributions towards their social security, when they work temporarily in each other’s territory.
        • Traditional Medicine: Dedicated provisions/ annexes are secured in agreements with Oman and EU.
        • Double Taxation related provisions negotiated in India-Australia ECTA, securing commitments to eliminate Double taxation on India's IT services.
    1. Trade promotion through schemes, and participation in and organization of international fairs/ exhibitions

SEPC, set up by the Department of Commerce, plays a key role in services trade promotion and undertakes market development, trade facilitation, policy advocacy, capacity building, buyer-seller engagement, international outreach and export-promotion activities across major services sectors. They are supported in this through financial assistance under the Export Promotion Mission of Government of India. Few of the recent activities undertaken by SEPC are highlighted below:

      • 2nd edition of Medical Value Tourism (MVT) Summit on 4-5 April 2025 organised with Tamil Nadu government, featuring hospitals, wellness centres, AYUSH centres and medical institutions from Tamil Nadu.
      • Indian Pavilions in association with relevant ministries and departments: at the Arabian Travel Market (ATM) 2025, from 28 April to 1 May 2025 at the Dubai World Trade Centre, Dubai; at Global Education & Training Exhibition (GETEX) held from 30th April 2025 – 2nd May 2025 at Dubai International Convention & Exhibition Centre, Dubai, UAE; at MIPCOM 2025 in Paris, France from 13-16 October 2025 on the theme "Waves Bazaar"; at Malaysia Health & Pharma Expo from 7-9th October 2025 in Kula Lumpur, Malaysia; at Tokyo Games Show from 24-26 September 2025 at Tokyo, Japan; and at GAMESCOM 2025 from 20-24th August 2025 at Cologne, Germany showcasing Indian companies’ capabilities in gaming and entertainment segments.
      • Organised events such as Future-Ready Logistics in India on 29th August 2025; International Conference on Transforming Higher Education & Skilling towards Viksit Bhat@2024 & Education Excellence Awards 2025 on 19th September 2025; Finolegal Convergence Summit 2025 on 5th December 2025 on the theme: “Regulation. Innovation. Globalization– Building India’s Legal–Fintech Edge”; and a National Dialogue on School Education Building Future- Ready Learners for a Skilled India on 13th December 2025 at New Delhi.

2288850.title: Update on NFHS-6
2288850.ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
2288850.body_html:
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Update on NFHS-6
NFHS-6 Shows Significant Improvements in Maternal and Child Health Indicators Across the Country
NFHS-6 Highlights Rising lifestyle diseases among Adults
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:55PM by PIB Delhi

Government has undertaken a comprehensive analysis of key findings of the latest National Family Health Survey (NFHS).

The major key findings are as follows: [from NFHS-5 (2019-21) to NFHS-6 (2023-24)]

  • Institutional deliveries increased from 88.6% to 90.6%.
  • ANC coverage increased from 92.6% to 95.9%, with mothers receiving at least four ANC visits rising from 58.5% to 65.2%.
  • Births attended by skilled health personnel improved from 89.4% to 91.3%.
  • Contraceptive Prevalence Rate increased from 66.7% to 69.1%.
  • At the same time, total unmet need (the proportion of people who want to avoid or delay pregnancy but are not using any method) has reduced from 9.4% to 8.5%, a direct reflection of increased CPR.
  • The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) has remained stable at 2, across NFHS-5 and NFHS-6, which is below the replacement level of 2.1, indicating sustained low fertility.
  • Full immunization coverage among children aged 12-23 months improved from 83.8% to 87.1%. (based on information from vaccination card)
  • Coverage of the second dose of measles-containing vaccine also increased significantly from 58.6% to 71.8%.
  • The most striking gain is recorded for the rotavirus vaccine, where coverage has more than doubled, from 36.4% to 85.4% between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6.
  • Stunting among children under five years declined from 35.5% to 29.3% and severe wasting declined from 7.7% to 5.2%.
  • NFHS-6 also notes a rise in obesity - a key risk factor for chronic NCDs — with 30.7% of women and 27.3% of men aged 15–49 years reported as overweight or obese.
  •  Blood sugar level - high or very high (>140 mg/dl) or taking medicine to control blood sugar among adults in population more than 15 years of age has increased in both women (13.5% to 17.8%) and men (15.6% to 20.9%).
  • Hypertension among Adults in population more than 15 years of age shows a decline in both women (21.3% to 19.4%) and men (24.0% to 22.1%).
  • Details on other public health indicators may be accessed through the reports: https://www.nfhsiips.in/nfhsuser/assets/National%20Family%20Health%20Survey%20(NFHS-6)%202023-2024%20Fact%20Sheets.pdf

The Union Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare, Shri. Prataprao Jadhav stated this in a written reply in the Lok Sabha today.

2288849.title: India and Israel Conclude Second Round of Negotiations for Proposed Free Trade Agreement
2288849.body_html:
Ministry of Commerce & Industry
India and Israel Conclude Second Round of Negotiations for Proposed Free Trade Agreement
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:54PM by PIB Delhi

India and Israel concluded the second round of negotiations for the proposed India-Israel Free Trade Agreement (FTA), held from 20 to 23 July 2026 at Vanijya Bhawan, New Delhi. During the four-day negotiations, both sides held detailed discussions across all areas of the proposed Agreement and continued to make progress towards a balanced, comprehensive and mutually beneficial FTA.

The Terms of Reference (ToR), signed in November 2025, continue to provide the structured framework for negotiations on the identified areas to strengthen bilateral trade, economic cooperation and the overall economic partnership between the two countries.

Total merchandise trade between India and Israel stood at USD 3.93 billion in FY 2025-26. The two countries share strong complementarities across several sectors, and the proposed FTA presents significant opportunities to further enhance bilateral trade, investment and economic integration.

During this round, technical experts from both sides held dedicated sessions covering trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, intellectual property rights, customs procedures and trade facilitation, economic cooperation, and other chapters under the proposed Agreement. The discussions were constructive and forward-looking, with both sides engaging in detailed technical deliberations aimed at narrowing gaps and identifying areas of convergence.

During the opening session, India's Chief Negotiator for the FTA, Additional Secretary, Department of Commerce, Shri Ajay Bhadoo reaffirmed India's commitment to negotiating a balanced, comprehensive and mutually beneficial agreement that would further strengthen bilateral trade and economic relations between the two countries. Israel's Chief Negotiator, Ms. Yifat Alon Perel, Senior Director, Trade Policy & Agreements and Deputy Trade Commissioner, Foreign Trade Administration, Ministry of Economy and Industry, appreciated the progress made since the first round of negotiations and emphasised the importance of maintaining the momentum towards achieving an ambitious and mutually beneficial outcome.

Both sides reiterated their commitment to working towards the early conclusion of a balanced, comprehensive and mutually beneficial FTA that will further deepen bilateral trade, investment and economic ties between India and Israel.

2288848.title: Update on ABDM
2288848.ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
2288848.body_html:
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Update on ABDM
Over 94.87 Crore ABHA IDs Created Under Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission as of 20 July 2026
ABDM Digital Registries Expand Nationwide with 5.36 Lakh Health Facilities and 10.09 Lakh Healthcare Professionals
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:54PM by PIB Delhi

As of 20th July 2026, under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), 94.87 crore ABHAs have been created across the country.

Under ABDM, Health Facility Registry (HFR) has been created which includes verified healthcare facilities such hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, blood banks etc. As of 20th July 2026, 5.36 lakh facilities are registered on the HFR. Similarly, the Healthcare Professionals Registry is a registry of verified healthcare professionals. As of 20th July 2026, 10.09 lakh healthcare professionals are registered on the HPR.

The state-wise and district-wise distribution, is available on the real-time ABDM dashboard at https://dashboard.abdm.gov.in/

A third-party evaluation study of the ABDM was conducted between June-August 2025. The key findings of the evaluation study are highlighted below :

● ABDM has reduced waiting times, enabled cost savings, and improved service access, particularly benefiting women and underserved populations.

● Considering the well-structured strategic foundation, robust digital infrastructure rollout, and effective stakeholder engagement across public and private sectors, ABDM has brought in efficiency in the health service delivery ecosystem.

● Unified Health Interface (UHI) serves as a key digital gateway under ABDM, facilitating seamless discovery and delivery of health services and significantly enhancing accessibility, convenience, and reach of healthcare services for citizens

● ABDM has shown impact by enhancing healthcare efficiency, accessibility, and affordability, especially for underserved groups. Its interoperable infrastructure and cross-sectoral collaborations have driven systemic shifts, through broader integration and measurable health outcomes which are key to sustaining long term success

‘Privacy by Design’ is one of the key guiding principles of ABDM and there is no centralised repository of health data. ABDM facilitates secure data exchange between the intended stakeholders on the ABDM network after the patient’s consent. Also, before integrating with ABDM, digital health applications are validated in a Sandbox environment, and they also undergo security audits like WASA (Web Application Security Audit) to ensure data security.

ABDM enables interoperability by establishing common health data standards and developing registries for individuals, health facilities, healthcare professionals, and other necessary components. This allows various digital health systems across both public and private healthcare ecosystems to exchange data across healthcare providers, even when they use different digital platforms.

Technical support is provided for integration of any digital health solution with ABDM, including public health programs. Several national and state public health programme platforms including Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), Nikshay, Reproductive and Child Health (RCH), Non-Communicable Diseases (NCD), Gujarat’s TECHO, Uttar Pradesh’s eKavach, Rajasthan’s Pregnancy, Child Tracking and Health Services Management (PCTS), Tamil Nadu CMCHIS (Comprehensive Health Insurance Scheme) are integrated with ABDM.

The Union Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare, Shri. Prataprao Jadhav stated this in a written reply in the Lok Sabha today.

2288846.title: Measures taken to curb Childhood Hypertension and Obesity
2288846.ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
2288846.body_html:
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Measures taken to curb Childhood Hypertension and Obesity
RBSK 2.0 Expanded to Cover 38 Childhood Health Conditions, Including Diabetes, Hypertension and Mental Health
Digital Tracking, Strengthened Mobile Health Teams and IEC Campaign Enhanced Delivery of RBSK 2.0
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:53PM by PIB Delhi

The Operational Guideliness of RBSK 2.0 of the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) has expanded the programmatic framework to cover 38 common health conditions. The revised guidelines include emerging child health priorities such as non-communicable diseases including diabetes and hypertension, mental health conditions, and behavioural concerns among children.

The existing Mobile Health Teams (MHTs) under RBSK are strengthened through additional support of human resources from other existing health programs under National Health Mission for screening in Schools and Anganwadi centres. A comprehensive preventive, promotive, and curative continuum of care approach is used for tracking and follow-up using a digital platform for effective implementation

To generate awareness among children and parents regarding lifestyle-related health issues, and to strengthen healthy lifestyle practices Information Education and Communication (IEC) materials like health booklet, videos, and posters have been developed, and shared with States/UTs for dissemination in the community.

The Union Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare, Smt. Anupriya Patel stated this in a written reply in the Lok Sabha today.

2288841.title: Television Rating Policy, 2026 to Strengthen Transparency, Independence and Accountability in India's TV Audience Measurement System
2288841.body_html:
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting
Television Rating Policy, 2026 to Strengthen Transparency, Independence and Accountability in India's TV Audience Measurement System
New Policy Reduces Net Worth Requirement, Expands Metered Homes and Introduces Periodic Establishment Surveys
Policy Mandates Independent Audits, Cross-Holding Restrictions and Graded Penalties to Ensure Credible TV Audience Measurement
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:50PM by PIB Delhi

The Ministry of Information & Broadcasting (MIB) has released the TV Ratings Policy 2026, which sets out comprehensive guidelines for regulating television ratings in India. The policy defines clear standards for the registration, operation, audit, and oversight of agencies providing TV rating services, with the aim of ensuring transparency, independence and accountability in audience measurement.

The TV Rating Policy 2026 replaced the existing Guidelines for TV Rating Agencies in India dated 16th January 2014.

The major reforms introduced under the Policy include:

  1. Reduction of net worth criteria from Rs. 20 Crores to Rs. 5 Crores;
  2. Technology-neutral audience measurement across multiple platforms including connected TVs and TV channels available on OTT Platforms;
  3. Increased sample size by expansion of metered homes from 50,000 to 80,000;
  4. Periodic establishment surveys every three years;
  5. Exclusion of landing page in computation of viewership data;
  6. Annual independent audits; and
  7. A graded penalty framework for non-compliance.

The prescribed safeguards include cross-holding restrictions, requirement of at least 33% independent directors on the board of the agency, prohibition of consultancy or advisory activities that may create conflicts of interest, security clearance requirements, audit and transparency obligations to ensure the functional and operational independence of rating agencies.

Under this Policy, any entity in the business of television ratings in India has to comply with certain additional requirements and to register under the new Policy.

As on date, no entity is registered under the new Policy. The Television Ratings Policy, 2026 places no restriction on the number of agencies that may be registered to provide TV rating services.

This information was provided by the Minister of State for Information and Broadcasting and Parliamentary Affairs, Dr. L. Murugan, in a written reply to an Unstarred Question in the Rajya Sabha raised by Dr. John Brittas.

2288840.title: Kargil Vijay Diwas 2026
2288840.body_html:
PIB Backgrounder
Kargil Vijay Diwas 2026
A Tribute to Valour, Sacrifice, and the Spirit of India
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:50PM by PIB Delhi

Kargil Vijay Diwas honours the courage, sacrifice, and unwavering resolve of the Bravehearts of Operation Vijay. It commemorates India's historic victory in the Kargil War and celebrates the spirit that safeguarded the Nation's sovereignty. The occasion also reflects Kargil's enduring legacy. It continues to strengthen India's military preparedness, inspire generations, and reinforce the Nation's unwavering commitment to its security.

When Courage Conquered the Peaks

The Kargil War stands among the greatest chapters in India's military history. It reflects unmatched bravery, grit, and determination. It remains a lasting symbol of national pride and inspiration.

This year, the nation marks the 27th Kargil Vijay Diwas with gratitude and reverence. It commemorates India's historic victory in 1999. Indian soldiers reclaimed the snow-covered heights of Kargil through extraordinary courage and unwavering resolve. On 26 July, the Tricolour once again flew proudly over the rugged mountains of Ladakh. It became a timeless symbol of sacrifice, valour, and India's unbreakable spirit.

The Kargil conflict began in May 1999. Intruders crossed the Line of Control and occupied Indian positions on commanding heights. Their aim was to cut the link between Kashmir and Ladakh. The larger objective was to force India into negotiations on the Kashmir dispute. But they underestimated the will of a nation.  India responded with Operation Vijay. The mission reflected meticulous planning, unwavering determination, and the indomitable spirit of Indian soldiers. After more than two months of intense fighting, every intruder was driven out. Every occupied position returned to Indian control.

Kargil Vijay Diwas honours every Braveheart who sacrificed everything for the motherland. Their sacrifice strengthened India's resolve to secure every inch of its territory. The conflict reshaped the nation's military preparedness and defence outlook for the years ahead. Its lessons continue to guide India's march towards a stronger and more self-reliant future. It reminds every Indian that courage, sacrifice, unity, and sovereignty will forever remain the nation's greatest strength.

The Road to Operation Vijay

The Kargil War began in the summer of 1999, soon after the Lahore Declaration. While much of India endured scorching heat, fierce battles unfolded across the icy heights of Kargil. Pakistani forces infiltrated Indian territory and occupied winter vacated posts on commanding ridges. The conflict tested courage, endurance, and sacrifice in one of the world's harshest battlefields. It remains the only conventional war fought between two nuclear armed nations.

The Infiltration

The intrusion was part of Pakistan's Operation Badr. Pakistani forces, disguised as Kashmiri terrorists, crossed the Line of Control and occupied Indian positions. Their aim was to cut the link between Kashmir and Ladakh. They also sought to isolate Indian Army troops on the Siachen Glacier. The larger objective was to force India into negotiations on the Kashmir dispute.

On 3 May 1999, local residents first reported suspicious movement in the Kargil sector. Reconnaissance patrols were immediately dispatched to verify the reports. Extensive patrolling and aerial surveillance soon revealed the scale of the occupation. The infiltrators had entrenched themselves on dominating heights overlooking the Srinagar to Leh Highway. Many positions stood above 5,000 metres, making every military operation exceptionally challenging.

Operation Vijay Begins

India responded with restraint, resolve, and determination. The government directed that the Line of Control would not be crossed. The mission was clear. Every occupied post had to be reclaimed.

The Indian Army launched Operation Vijay to evict the intruders. The Indian Air Force joined the campaign through Operation Safed Sagar on 26 May 1999. The Indian Navy also deployed in full strength, demonstrating India's resolve across every domain. Together, the three Services executed a coordinated campaign.

Operation Vijay followed the strategy of contain, evict, and deny. Priority was given to recapturing the heights dominating the Srinagar to Leh Highway. Additional troops, artillery, engineers, specialised equipment, and logistics were rapidly inducted. Soldiers climbed near vertical cliffs under relentless enemy fire. They battled freezing temperatures, thin air, and unforgiving terrain.

Battles That Changed the Course of the War

The Battle of Tololing marked one of the first major breakthroughs of the campaign. Indian troops launched their assault in the last week of May 1999. Point 4590 and Tololing was fully recaptured on 13 June, opening the way for further advances.

The Battle of Tiger Hill became one of the defining moments of the war. Tiger Hill was among the highest peaks in the Dras sector and one of the Indian Army's most important objectives. After a daring assault, the peak was recaptured on 4 July 1999, significantly shifting the momentum in India's favour.

Fierce fighting also took place at Point 4875, Batalik, Mushkoh Valley, and Kaksar. Indian soldiers fought peak by peak to reclaim every occupied position. After nearly three months of relentless operations, every occupied Indian post was recaptured. India secured victory without crossing the Line of Control, earning global respect for its restraint, professionalism, and unwavering resolve.

A Victory That Inspired a Nation

The Kargil War became a defining chapter in India's history. It showcased the extraordinary courage of Indian soldiers and united the nation in pride. On 14 July 1999, then Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee addressed the nation and declared Operation Vijay a success. He paid tribute to the courage, sacrifice, and unwavering resolve of the Armed Forces.

The victory reaffirmed that every inch of Indian territory would be defended at any cost. It strengthened the nation's faith in its Armed Forces and inspired generations of Indians.

The Bravery That Defined Kargil

The victory in Kargil was made possible by countless acts of courage. Every peak reclaimed reflected the determination and sacrifice of India's Armed Forces. While every soldier contributed to Operation Vijay, several acts of exceptional gallantry became defining moments of the conflict. Heroes such as Grenadier Yogendra Singh Yadav, Captain Vikram Batra, Captain Vijyant Thapar, and many others became symbols of courage and selfless service.

The nation honoured this extraordinary valour with its highest military decorations. 4 soldiers were awarded the Param Vir Chakra, India's highest gallantry award. 9 received the Maha Vir Chakra, while 55 were honoured with the Vir Chakra. 1 soldier was conferred the Sarvottam Yudh Seva Medal. 6 received the Uttam Yudh Seva Medal, and 8 were awarded the Yudh Seva Medal. The Sena Medal was awarded to 83 personnel, while 24 received the Vayu Sena Medal. These honours reflect the extraordinary courage, leadership, and sacrifice displayed during the Kargil War.

Read the inspiring stories of these Bravehearts Click To Read More Here.

From Battlefield Lessons to a Stronger Defence Ecosystem

The Kargil War became a turning point in India's defence journey. It highlighted the need for stronger coordination, faster modernisation, and greater self-reliance. Over the years, India has undertaken wide ranging reforms to strengthen its defence ecosystem and build indigenous capabilities. Today, these efforts are shaping a stronger, more capable, and increasingly Atmanirbhar military.

Some of the key reforms and initiatives are outlined below:

Establishment of the Department of Military Affairs

The Department of Military Affairs was created as a part of Higher Defence Management Reforms. It functions under the CDS, who serves as its Secretary. The department promotes jointmanship among the Army, Navy, and Air Force. It also supports coordinated defence doctrines, planning, and procedures across the three Services.

Creation of the Chief of Defence Staff

One of the most significant reforms was the creation of the post of Chief of Defence Staff (CDS). The CDS serves as the single point military adviser to the Government. The role also promotes greater jointness among the Army, Navy, and Air Force. General Bipin Rawat became India's first CDS in 2020. The post is currently held by General N. S. Raja Subramani.

Foreign Direct Investment in Defence

The defence industry was opened to private sector participation. The FDI limit has increased to 74 per cent through the Automatic Route for new defence industrial licences. It also allows up to 100 per cent through the Government Route where modern technology is introduced. As of March 2026, the sector has attracted FDI worth ₹6,670.59 crore. The Government also promotes co-development and co-production with Foreign Original Equipment Manufacturers to strengthen advanced defence manufacturing.

Enhanced Defence Budget

India's defence allocation has risen steadily from ₹2.53 lakh crore in 2013–14 to ₹7.85 lakh crore in 2026–27. Capital expenditure has also increased from ₹94,587.95 crore in 2014–15 to ₹2.19 lakh crore in 2026–27. These investments are strengthening long term military capability through modern equipment, infrastructure, and strategic assets.

Growth in Defence Production and Exports

India's defence production reached an all-time high of ₹1.78 lakh crore in 2025–26, almost four times higher than ₹46,429 crore in 2014–15.

Defence exports increased from ₹686 crore in 2013–14 to ₹38,424 crore in 2025–26, a rise of more than 56 times. Today, Indian defence products are exported to over 80 countries. Driven by Make in India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat, India is steadily emerging as a defence manufacturing nation. Nearly 65 per cent of defence equipment is now produced within the country, compared to an earlier import dependence of 65 to 70 per cent.

Accelerating Indigenous Defence Manufacturing

The Ministry of Defence launched the Srijan Defence Portal. The portal connects Defence Public Sector Undertakings and Service Headquarters with industries, MSMEs, and startups for indigenisation. Positive Indigenisation Lists were introduced in 2021 under the Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative.

Till May 2026, five Positive Indigenisation Lists covering 5,012 items of DPSUs have been notified. More than 15,700 defence items, including 3,204 Positive Indigenisation List items, have been indigenised during the last five years. DPSUs have placed domestic orders worth ₹9,782 crore, strengthening MSMEs, startups, research institutions, and India's defence manufacturing ecosystem.

Defence Industrial Corridors Driving Regional Manufacturing

Defence Industrial Corridors have emerged as key growth centres for defence manufacturing, strengthening regional supply chains and fostering integrated industrial ecosystems. By April 2026, the Uttar Pradesh Defence Industrial Corridor had attracted investment commitments worth ₹42,057 crore, with grounded investments of ₹4,409 crore, supported by the establishment of the Defence Technology & Test Centre (DTTC) to enhance testing and innovation capabilities. During the same period, the Tamil Nadu Defence Industrial Corridor attracted investments worth ₹32,699 crore, with actual investments reaching ₹6,446 crore. Together, these corridors are accelerating industrial infrastructure development, expanding domestic manufacturing capacity, and generating new employment opportunities.

Agnipath Scheme

The Agnipath Scheme was launched to recruit young men and women into the Armed Forces as Agniveers for a four-year service period. The scheme aims to create a youthful, tech-savvy, and combat-ready military force with a modern outlook. Agniveers receive military training, specialised skill development, and educational opportunities through partnerships with institutions such as IGNOU and NIOS. The scheme also provides nationally recognised skill certificates and career pathways after service.

The legacy of Kargil continues to inspire reforms that are strengthening India's Armed Forces and reinforcing the nation's security.

Towards a Future Ready Military

The character of warfare has changed significantly since the Kargil War. Modern conflicts demand advanced technology, superior firepower, and rapid decision making. India has strengthened its military capabilities through the induction of modern platforms and the development of next generation defence technologies. These capabilities are enhancing operational readiness across land, air, sea, space, and emerging domains.

Some of the key platforms and emerging technologies driving this transformation are outlined below.

Modern Platforms in Service

India has inducted advanced platforms across the three Services to strengthen combat capability and enhance operational effectiveness.

  • Arjun Mk IA Battle Tank: The Arjun Mk IA battle tank was inducted into the Indian Army in February 2021. It strengthened India's indigenous armoured capability.
  • INS Vikrant: India's first indigenous aircraft carrier, INS Vikrant, was commissioned on 2 September 2022. It marked a major milestone in maritime capability and self-reliance.
  • Rafale Fighter Aircraft: By 2030, India will operate 62 Rafale fighter aircraft, including 26 Rafale M aircraft. India will become the first country after France to operate both variants.
  • Apache and Chinook Helicopters: The induction of Apache attack helicopters and Chinook heavy lift helicopters has enhanced combat capability and strategic airlift capacity.
  • Integration of Drone Warfare: India has integrated drone warfare into its military doctrine. Drones now strengthen surveillance, reconnaissance, precision operations, and battlefield effectiveness.
  • BrahMos Cruise Missile: The first successful BrahMos launch took place on 12 June 2001. This multi-platform supersonic cruise missile can be launched from land, sea, and air. It has a range of up to 290 kilometres and travels at nearly Mach 2.8.
  • Project 17A Stealth Frigates: Project 17A is the Indian Navy's advanced stealth frigate programme to build seven next generation guided missile warships. These frigates are designed for anti-air, anti-surface, and anti-submarine warfare.
  • Sandhayak Class Survey Vessels: The Sandhayak class survey vessels strengthen the Indian Navy's hydrographic capability by mapping the seabed and coastal waters. The indigenous class comprises INS Sandhayak, INS Nirdeshak, INS Ikshak, and INS Sanshodhak, enhancing India's maritime survey and navigation capabilities.
  • Arnala Class Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft: The Arnala class strengthens the Indian Navy's coastal defence and anti-submarine warfare capability. The indigenous eight ship class comprises INS Arnala, INS Androth, INS Anjadip, INS Amini, INS Abhay, INS Agray, INS Akshay, and the recently commissioned INS Ajay. INS Arnala is the largest waterjet propelled warship inducted into the Indian Navy. Click To Read More: Guardians of India's Maritime Frontiers

Emerging Technologies and Strategic Capabilities

India is investing in advanced technologies to prepare its Armed Forces for the battlefields of tomorrow.

  • Mission Shakti: On 27 March 2019, India successfully conducted Mission Shakti, an anti-satellite missile test, from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island. With this achievement, India joined the exclusive group of nations possessing anti-satellite capability.
  • Artificial Intelligence in Defence: In 2022, India introduced 75 Artificial Intelligence based technologies for surveillance, cyber security, logistics, autonomous systems, and battlefield support.
  • Mission Divyastra: On 11 March 2024, India successfully tested a long range missile carrying multiple warheads against different targets under Mission Divyastra.
  • Pinaka Long Range Guided Rocket: The maiden flight test of the Pinaka Long Range Guided Rocket was successfully conducted on 29 December 2025. The rocket demonstrated a maximum range of 120 kilometres and achieved textbook precision during the trial.
  • Advanced Air Defence System: On 23 August 2025, DRDO successfully tested an advanced air defence system. It combines missile interceptors, short range air defence weapons, and laser based technologies.
  • Hypersonic Missile Technologies: India has advanced next generation propulsion systems for hypersonic missiles. In January 2026, DRDO completed a successful long duration scramjet combustor ground test. A new Hypersonic Wind Tunnel in Hyderabad now supports future high speed missile development.
  • Kusha Long Range Surface to Air Missile: In July 2026, DRDO successfully conducted the maiden flight test of the Kusha missile. It intercepted a simulated high speed aerial threat. The system can neutralise fighter jets, missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and large enemy aircraft across a wide range and altitude. It has been developed indigenously by DRDO laboratories and industry partners.
  • Long Range Land Attack Cruise Missile: In June 2026, DRDO successfully flight tested the Long Range Land Attack Cruise Missile from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island. The missile successfully achieved all test objectives. It is an indigenously developed system with all major sub systems developed by DRDO laboratories and Indian industry partners.
  • Netra Airborne Early Warning and Control System: In June 2026, DRDO handed over the Final Operational Clearance certificate for the indigenous Netra Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) system. The system was developed jointly by DRDO, the Indian Air Force, and industry partners. It significantly enhances airborne surveillance, situational awareness, and battle management capabilities.

From modern combat platforms to next generation technologies, India continues to build a future ready military. These capabilities strengthen deterrence, enhance operational preparedness, and reinforce the Nation's ability to safeguard its sovereignty.

Kargil's Enduring Legacy

A stronger military is most meaningful when matched by unwavering resolve. Since Kargil, India has steadily strengthened both its defence capabilities and its response to evolving security challenges. This approach continues to shape the Nation's security doctrine and operational posture.

Surgical Strikes and Balakot Air Strikes

India's response to cross border terrorism has entered a new phase over the last decade. Following the Uri terror attack, India conducted Surgical Strikes on 28 and 29 September 2016. The operation inflicted heavy losses on terrorists and their protectors across the Line of Control. It marked a more proactive approach against cross border terrorism.

A few years later, on 14 February 2019, the Pulwama terror attack claimed 40 CRPF jawans. India’s response came swiftly. On 26 February 2019, in an intelligence-led operation, the Balakot airstrikes eliminated a large number of Jaish-e-Mohammad terrorists. The facility targeted was located far from civilian areas and headed by Maulana Yousuf Azhar, brother-in-law of JeM chief Masood Azhar. These pre-emptive actions showed the world that India would no longer tolerate proxy war through terrorism.

Operation SINDOOR

India's evolving military doctrine was further demonstrated during Operation SINDOOR in May 2025. The operation followed the terrorist attack on civilians in Pahalgam. The Armed Forces struck nine terrorist camps in Pakistan and Pakistan occupied Jammu and Kashmir.

The operation relied on accurate intelligence, drones, loitering munitions, and layered air defence. Key Jaish-e-Mohammad and Lashkar-e-Taiba command centres were destroyed. The strikes resulted in over 100 terrorists killed in action. Those eliminated included individuals linked to IC-814 hijack and Pulwama blast like Yusuf Azhar, Abdul Malik Rauf and Mudassir Ahmad.

Pakistan launched drone and missile attacks on 7 and 8 May. India's integrated air defence systems intercepted them swiftly. The response showcased India's net centric warfare capabilities and integrated counter unmanned aerial systems grid.

From Kargil to Operation SINDOOR, India's response to terrorism has become increasingly proactive, precise, and decisive.

Celebrating the Spirit of Kargil

While the legacy of Kargil continues to shape India's military resolve, it also lives on in the Nation's collective memory. Every year, Kargil Vijay Diwas brings the country together to honour the courage and sacrifice of the Bravehearts of 1999. Across the country, commemorative events are being organised to pay tribute to their supreme sacrifice. These initiatives celebrate their legacy while inspiring future generations with the values of courage, duty, and patriotism.
 

Shaurya Vijay Yatra

Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh flagged off the 13-day Shaurya Vijay Yatra on 14 July 2026. The motorcycle expedition began at the National War Memorial in New Delhi. It will conclude at the Kargil War Memorial in Dras after covering 1,900 kilometres. 28 riders, including serving and retired defence personnel with their families, are participating. The expedition carries the motto "One Ride, One Nation, One Salute."

Wheels of Valour: Sanchar Shakti

As part of the nationwide Wheels of Valour: Sanchar Shakti expedition, the Corps of Signals Dare Devils created a new world record on 1 July 2026. Ten riders performed on two motorcycles inside the Atal Tunnel. They completed the 9.8-kilometre tunnel in 9 minutes and 47.97 seconds. The feat honoured the spirit of Kargil Vijay Diwas while showcasing military skill, endurance, and teamwork.

 

Tiger Hill Expedition 2026

The Indian Army and the Civil Administration, Dras, organised the Tiger Hill Expedition on 17 July 2026. The initiative promoted military tourism while preserving the legacy of the Kargil War. Eleven trained local trekking guides also participated, creating livelihood opportunities for local youth.

Honouring Veterans and Bravehearts

On 16 July 2026, Tri Services Ex Servicemen and their families visited the Kargil War Memorial and Heritage Hut Museum. The visit honoured the Bravehearts of Kargil and strengthened the enduring bond among veterans, serving personnel, and their families.

Ex Servicemen, school children, and villagers also paid tribute at the Khalubar War Memorial on 10 July 2026. The ceremony reaffirmed the enduring values of patriotism, courage, and selfless service.

Commemorative Treks and Military Displays

On 13 July 2026, 137 soldiers undertook a commemorative trek to Point 5140, also known as Gun Hill. The trek honoured the Regiment of Artillery for its decisive contribution during Operation Vijay.

Indian Army also organised a Weapon and Equipment Display at Hanle. The exhibition showcased modern weapons, drones, and surveillance systems. It highlighted the Indian Army's technological capabilities and operational readiness in high altitude areas.

 

Leh to Dras Motorcycle Expedition

On 12 and 13 July 2026, Indian Army riders undertook a motorcycle expedition from Leh to the Kargil War Memorial in Dras. The riders crossed the challenging Fotu La, Namika La, and Umba La passes. The expedition honoured the Bravehearts of Operation Vijay while demonstrating endurance, camaraderie, and military spirit.

These commemorative events ensure that the legacy of Kargil continues to inspire every generation with the timeless ideals of courage, sacrifice, and service to the Nation.

The Victory That Lives On

Twenty-seven years later, the echoes of Kargil still resonate across the Nation. The victory stands as an enduring symbol of courage, sacrifice, and unwavering patriotism. Every peak recaptured reminds us that India's sovereignty is non-negotiable and will be defended at any cost. Inspired by the valour of its Bravehearts, India has emerged stronger, better prepared, and increasingly self-reliant. As the Nation salutes the heroes of Kargil, it also renews its solemn resolve to uphold their legacy. Their courage will forever inspire generations to serve the Nation with honour, duty, and unwavering commitment.

2288839.title: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) observed Swachhata Pakhwada  from 1st to 15th July,2026 across the country
2288839.body_html:
Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation
Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) observed Swachhata Pakhwada from 1st to 15th July,2026 across the country
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:45PM by PIB Delhi

The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) observed Swachhata Pakhwada 2026 from 1st to 15th July 2026 with active participation of all Divisions, Attached /Subordinate/ Autonomous Organisations and Field level Offices of the Ministry  located across the country.

The Swachhata Pakhwada commenced with the administration of the Swachhata Pledge and a wide cleanliness drive aimed at reinforcing the commitment towards cleanliness, environmental sustainability and efficient workplace management.

A comprehensive day-wise action plan was prepared covering activities such as office cleanliness drives, record weeding and review of old files, disposal of obsolete and unserviceable items, digital housekeeping and promotion of e-office practices. Special emphasis was laid on improving office surroundings and enhancing workplace hygiene.

During the fortnight, various Divisions and Offices of the Ministry as well as field offices of MoSPI located across the country organized a wide range of activities including plantation drives, Swachhata awareness campaigns, seminars, workshops, quiz competitions, essay and poster competitions, rallies, shramdaan programmes and community outreach initiatives aimed at promoting public awareness on cleanliness and environmental protection.

The Ministry also undertook initiatives related to reduction of single-use plastic, waste segregation, recycling and sustainable waste management practices in line with the objectives of the Government of India's Swachh Bharat Mission.

As part of the Pakhwada, best practices and innovative initiatives undertaken by various Divisions and Regional Offices were documented and disseminated across the Ministry to encourage wider adoption and institutionalization of successful cleanliness initiatives.

The Swachhata Pakhwada concluded on 15 July 2026 with activities undertaken, sharing of achievements and recognition of significant contributions made by various offices and officials towards strengthening the culture of cleanliness within the Ministry.

The Ministry reaffirms its commitment towards the vision of a cleaner, healthier and more sustainable India and calls upon all officials and stakeholders to actively participate in the Swachhata movement.

"Swachhata is not merely an activity, but a collective responsibility and a way of life."

Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:16PM by PIB Delhi

The Government of India has reiterated that it has put in place a robust mechanism to ensure the timely and adequate availability of fertilizers across the country during every cropping season. Through advance planning, continuous monitoring, and coordinated action with State Governments, adequate availability of all major fertilizers viz. Urea, DAP, MOP and NPKS—has been maintained across the States during the ongoing Kharif 2026 season.

To ensure seamless fertilizer availability, the Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with State Governments, assesses State-wise and month-wise fertilizer requirements before every cropping season. Based on these projections, the Department of Fertilizers allocates fertilizer supplies through monthly supply plans and continuously monitors availability. The movement of subsidized fertilizers is tracked through the Integrated Fertilizer Management System (iFMS), while regular weekly review meetings with State Agriculture officials help address emerging supply issues. Distribution within States is managed by the respective State Governments. Further, The Government has implemented Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) Scheme w.e.f. 01.04.2010 for Phosphatic and Potassic (P&K) Fertilizers.  Under NBS policy, MRP of P&K fertilizers are decontrolled and companies are free to fix MRP as per their business dynamics at a reasonable level. The NBS subsidy is provided to manufacturer / importer on notified P&K fertilizers on its PoS sale during the season, depending on their nutrient content to ensure availability of fertilizers to farmers. The volatility in international prices of key fertilizers and raw materials is considered while fixing NBS rates for P&K fertilizers so that fertilizers remain affordable to the farmers.

To make DAP which is a key fertilizer, available at affordable price of Rs. 1350 per 50 kg bag, special provisions like Rs. 3500 per MT to cover ‘Other Costs’ which includes costs incurred from factory gate to farm gate, advantage / disadvantage due to increase / decrease in international prices, provision for GST component included in the MRP and provision for reasonable return @ 4% of net MRP (MRP-GST) have been extended to both imported and domestic DAP and imported TSP over and above NBS subsidy for Kharif 2026 season to keep the prices of fertilizers stable.  

Government promotes balanced use of fertilizer through Soil Health & Fertility scheme. The scheme is being implemented since 2014-15 to provide Soil Health Cards (SHCs) for all farm holdings, to promote balanced and integrated nutrient management for improving productivity and soil fertility.

  • Soil samples are processed as per standard procedures and analysed for parameters such as pH, Electrical Conductivity, Organic Carbon, available Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium, Sulphur, and micronutrients (Zinc, Copper, Iron, Manganese & Boron).
  • Since 2014-15, 26.09 crore Soil Health Cards have been generated/ distributed as on date across the country.
  • In addition to state soil labs above, 1020 school mini soil labs are also established in the country under school soil health programme.
  • Under the scheme, Rs. 2153.29 Crore fund has been released so far since inception.
  • 93781 farmer’s trainings, 6.80 lakh demonstrations, 7425 farmer’s melas/ campaigns on soil health card recommendations have been organized across the country.
  • 1351166 ha area also covered under Promotion & Distribution of Micronutrients in the scheme.
  • National Productivity Council (NPC), New Delhi carried out a study 'Soil Testing Infrastructure for Faster Delivery of SHC in India' in 2017 in 76 districts of 19 States including Madhya Pradesh covering 170 soil testing labs and 1700 farmers. As a result of application of fertilizer and micronutrients as per SHC recommendations, there has been a decrease of use of chemical fertilizer application in the range of 8-10% was found. Overall 5-6% increase in the yield of crops was reported, due to application of fertilizer and micronutrients as per SHC.
  • An impact study of Soil Health & Fertility Scheme (November 2017) was conducted by National Institute of Agricultural Extension Management (MANAGE), Hyderabad. As per report, about 62.8% of the farmers use fertilizers according to the recommendations on the SHC.  The cost per acre reduced by 4 to 10 % due to low fertilizer use. Crop yields increased for majority of the crops, although moderately. Overall, paddy farmers reduced use of urea by 9%, Diammonium Phosphate (DAP)/Single Super Phosphate by 7%, but increased use of Potassium by 20%.
  • There was substantial decline in fertilizer use especially urea and DAP in paddy and cotton resulted in decreased cost of cultivation per unit area.

Further, NITI Aayog has conducted a study on the Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) Scheme. The evaluation notes that the Scheme has several conceptual strengths, including the promotion of balanced fertilization through nutrient-linked subsidies, expansion of coverage to 28 fertilizer grades, and comparatively lower subsidy requirements than urea. The study also highlights that there is scope for further strengthening the effectiveness of the Scheme by addressing aspects such as the inclusion of urea within the NBS framework, further streamlining operational processes, reducing import dependence, improving affordability for small and marginal farmers.

This information was provided by Hon’ble Minister of Chemicals & Fertilizers Shri Jagat Prakash Nadda, , in a written reply to a question in the Lok Sabha today.

2288817.title: NHA Convenes BRICS Dialogue on Strengthening Continuum of Care Through Digital Health and Responsible AI
2288817.ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
2288817.body_html:
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
NHA Convenes BRICS Dialogue on Strengthening Continuum of Care Through Digital Health and Responsible AI
Continuity of Care is the True Measure of Whether Digital Health and AI are Serving Citizens: Union Health Secretary
Over 940 million ABHA IDs and 1 billion Linked Digital Health Records Power India's Digital Health Ecosystem: Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava
Panel Discusses Digital Public Infrastructure and AI as Key Enablers of Connected, Patient-Centric Healthcare Across BRICS
Posted On: 24 JUL 2026 3:00PM by PIB Delhi

As part of the 16th BRICS Health Ministers' Meeting, a side event titled "From Digital Health Records to AI-Enabled Healthcare: Strengthening the Continuum of Care Through Interoperable Data Infrastructure and Responsible Artificial Intelligence" was organised today, by National Health Authority, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, bringing together policymakers, technical experts and health leaders from BRICS countries to deliberate on the transformative role of digital health infrastructure and responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) in delivering seamless, patient-centric healthcare.

The dialogue was anchored in the findings of the BRICS Health Track Technical Working Group 4 (TWG-4) Compendium on Continuum of Care, which underscores the importance of coordinated and uninterrupted health service delivery across different levels of care, healthcare providers and BRICS member states. The Compendium highlights that while continuity of care remains a shared policy objective, its effective implementation is often constrained by the lack of interoperable digital health infrastructure capable of supporting seamless exchange of health information across the patient care journey.

In her keynote address, Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava said that the discussions held over the past two days had reflected the collective commitment of BRICS countries to strengthening resilient, equitable and future-ready health systems. She noted that health cooperation remains one of the strongest pillars of the BRICS partnership, founded on mutual learning, shared innovation and a common commitment to achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC).

Emphasising that continuity of care lies at the heart of every health system, she said the fundamental challenge before all countries is to ensure that a citizen's healthcare journey—from prevention and diagnosis to treatment, rehabilitation and long-term follow-up—remains connected rather than fragmented across institutions, providers and geographies. She observed that continuity of care is the true measure of whether digital health and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are delivering meaningful benefits to citizens.

The Union Health Secretary stated that while no country can build the future of AI-enabled healthcare in isolation, BRICS nations share common challenges, including large and diverse populations, significant rural-urban disparities, a growing burden of chronic and non-communicable diseases, and stretched health workforces. These challenges, she said, make interoperable digital health infrastructure and responsible AI essential tools for strengthening integrated and people-centric healthcare delivery.

Highlighting the importance of interoperable digital health records, she said that a person's health journey spans multiple providers and institutions, making it imperative that health information travels securely and seamlessly with the individual. Built on interoperability, open standards and robust governance, digital health records help bridge information gaps between healthcare providers, improve clinical decision-making, reduce duplication of services, strengthen referrals and follow-up, and preserve the continuity of care.

Speaking on the role of AI, Smt. Srivastava said that responsible AI is already strengthening healthcare delivery by identifying patients at risk of dropping out of chronic disease management programmes, supporting early interventions, and providing clinical decision support to frontline and community health workers in remote and underserved areas. However, she emphasised that AI is only as effective as the quality of the digital public infrastructure on which it is built, and that trusted, interoperable and citizen-centric digital health systems must remain the foundation of AI-enabled healthcare.

Sharing India's experience, the Union Health Secretary highlighted the progress made under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) in creating a federated Digital Public Infrastructure for health. She informed delegates that India has created over 940 million ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) IDs, issued unique digital identities to more than one million healthcare professionals and over five lakh health facilities, while enabling citizens to securely access more than one billion linked digital health records across the continuum of care.

She also referred to India's recently launched SAHI (Strategic Framework for AI in Healthcare), unveiled during the AI India Impact Summit earlier this year, which provides a framework for the responsible adoption of AI to strengthen healthcare delivery while ensuring ethics, transparency, safety and citizen trust.

The Union Health Secretary emphasised that India's experience was being shared not as a model to be replicated, but as one example among many represented within BRICS. She called for deeper collaboration among member countries on interoperable standards, digital public infrastructure, governance frameworks for responsible AI, cybersecurity, health workforce capacity building, and collaborative research and innovation.

Welcoming the release of the BRICS Technical Working Group-4 Compendium on Digital Health Architecture for Continuum of Care, she described it as a significant milestone reflecting the collective expertise and innovation of BRICS nations. She congratulated all member countries and the Technical Working Group for developing the compendium, which demonstrates that despite diverse health systems, BRICS countries are united by a shared vision of connected, equitable and future-ready healthcare.

Concluding her address, Smt. Srivastava said that while digital health records provide the foundation, responsible AI offers the opportunity to redefine continuity of care for present and future generations.

Speaking at the Occasion, Chief Executive Officer, National Health Authority (NHA), Shri Sunil Kumar Barnwal delivered a detailed presentation on the BRICS Technical Working Group-4 (TWG-4) Compendium on Digital Health Architecture for Continuum of Care, outlining its key findings and recommendations. He explained that the compendium provides a comprehensive assessment of the current state of digital health ecosystems across BRICS countries and identifies the critical building blocks required to achieve seamless continuity of care through interoperable digital health infrastructure.

Presenting a comparative analysis of the digital health landscape across BRICS nations, Shri Barnwal highlighted the unique strengths and innovations demonstrated by each member country while also identifying the common challenges faced across the grouping. These include fragmented health information systems, limited interoperability, uneven digital maturity across regions, growing burden of chronic and non-communicable diseases, workforce constraints, and the need for robust data governance frameworks.

He emphasised that despite the diversity of health systems, BRICS countries share a common aspiration to build connected, patient-centric and resilient healthcare systems. The compendium, he noted, offers a practical framework for strengthening the continuum of care by promoting interoperable digital public infrastructure, adoption of open standards, secure and consent-based data exchange, and the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence.

The side event also featured a high-level panel discussion with delegates and experts from BRICS member countries and partner nations, who exchanged experiences and best practices on strengthening the continuum of care through interoperable digital health infrastructure and responsible Artificial Intelligence.

The discussion highlighted how countries are leveraging digital public infrastructure to improve continuity of care across diverse healthcare settings. Delegates from Brazil shared their experience with the National Health Data Network (RNDS), which has transformed the country's healthcare ecosystem from paper-based referrals to a unified national health information exchange. They also highlighted the expansion of telehealth services, now reaching nearly 80 per cent of municipalities, significantly improving access to specialist healthcare in remote and underserved regions, including the Amazon.

Representatives from Indonesia outlined the rapid scale-up of the country's Integrated Primary Health Care model across thousands of Puskesmas (primary health centres). They also discussed the implementation of the SATUSEHAT digital health platform, which has been adapted to support continuity of care across Indonesia's geographically dispersed archipelago of more than 17,000 islands despite connectivity challenges.

The panel underscored that while Artificial Intelligence presents immense opportunities for improving healthcare delivery, its safe and effective deployment depends on high-quality, interoperable health data and locally validated clinical evidence. Participants stressed the need for BRICS countries to invest in robust governance frameworks, data quality, interoperability standards, validation mechanisms, cybersecurity, health workforce capacity building and sustainable financing before scaling AI-enabled healthcare solutions.

The dialogue reaffirmed the collective commitment of BRICS countries to harness digital innovation and responsible AI for building resilient, inclusive and people-centric health systems, while advancing universal health coverage and strengthening continuity of care across the health ecosystem.

Deputy Minister of Health Vladimir Zelensky, Russia; Mr. Arthur Fernandes da Silva, Brazil; Dr. Hiwot Solomon, Ethiopia; Dr. Harditya Suryawanto, Indonesia; Dr. Grace Achungura, Team lead Health Systems in WHO-India; Ministers, Senior Officers and Delegates from the BRICS member and partner nations participated in the event.
