2287845.title: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act
2287845.body_html:
PIB Backgrounder
Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act
Transparency, Sovereignty, and Democratic Accountability
FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS (FAQs)
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:58PM by PIB Delhi

Q. What is the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA)?

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act governs the acceptance and utilisation of foreign contribution received from a ‘foreign source’, as defined in the Act. Foreign contribution may take the form of an article, currency or a foreign security and also includes specified income arising from such contribution.

Administered by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), the Act does three things: it identifies who may accept foreign contributions and on what conditions; it specifies how that money must be received, accounted for, and reported; and it restricts a narrow, defined set of foreign-funded activities that could affect India's sovereignty, security or public order. The law has its origins in 1976 and has been strengthened through successive amendments. The law was replaced with a new law in 2010 which was later amended in 2016, 2018, 2020 and now 2026.

Q. Does FCRA prohibit NGOs and civil society organisations from receiving foreign donations?

No. FCRA does not impose a general prohibition on foreign donations. It permits eligible associations to receive foreign contribution after obtaining registration or prior permission and requires such contribution to be received, utilised and reported in the prescribed manner.

Many democracies have also introduced laws to improve transparency and accountability in relation to foreign funding or foreign influence like United States (FARA), Australia (FITS), the United Kingdom (FIRS) and Canada (FITAA), none of which are described internationally as "bans". The scope and legal design of those laws differ from country to country, but they reflect a common concern that cross-border funding and influence should be transparent and subject to appropriate safeguards.

In 2024-25, around 16,200 associations were actively registered and received approximately Rs 22,963 crore in foreign contribution, hardly the footprint of a prohibition. The law is best understood as a registration and disclosure regime for foreign-directed activity, not a permission-to-exist regime for civil society.

Q. What are the core objectives of FCRA?

The FCRA is built on several consistent principles.

  • Transparency: every organisation receiving foreign contributions must register, receive funds through a verifiable banking channel, and disclose amounts received, donors, and purposes.
  • Accountability: recipients must file annual audited returns that are to be filed online.
  • Sovereignty: contributions from abroad that could adversely affect India's sovereignty, democratic institutions, electoral processes, public order or national security are regulated. Enabling Genuine
  • Work: legitimate international cooperation in education, healthcare, poverty alleviation, disaster relief, cultural exchange, scientific research, and environmental work continues unimpeded.
  • Public Confidence: when citizens know that foreign funding is registered, disclosed, and audited, it builds trust in the voluntary sector and in the organisations themselves.

Q. How has FCRA evolved since it was first enacted?

India enacted the first FCRA in 1976. A 1984 amendment made registration with the Home Ministry mandatory for all NGOs receiving foreign funds. The current FCRA, 2010, replaced the 1976 Act with stronger compliance architecture.

The 2020 amendment introduced mandatory Aadhaar/passport identification for office-bearers, confined foreign contributions to a single SBI New Delhi account, prohibited sub-granting, cut the administrative-expense ceiling from 50% to 20%, and extended the suspension period.

The 2022 Rules raised the limit on contributions from relatives abroad from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 10 lakh. The 2024-25 Rules allowed unspent administrative-expense allocations to be carried forward and strengthened renewal documentation. Each reform has moved in the same direction — greater disclosure, stronger accountability, and improved governance.

Q. How does FCRA registration work in practice?

An organisation wishing to receive foreign contribution must either obtain an FCRA registration, available to organisations operational for at least three years or apply for prior permission for a defined project. Both routes require identity verification, a description of proposed activities, and disclosure of office-bearers.

All foreign contributions must first arrive in a single designated FCRA account at the State Bank of India's New Delhi Main Branch, creating one auditable entry point. From this account, funds may be moved to operational accounts for legitimate programme use.

Registration certificates are valid for five years and must be renewed, with a compliance review at the renewal stage.

Q. What are the financial discipline requirements for FCRA registered organisations?

Organisations must declare the purposes for which they are receiving foreign contributions and spend the money on those declared purposes.

No more than 20% of the annual foreign contribution may be used for administrative expenses, the remaining 80% must go to the activities for which the funding was received.

Every registered organisation shall file an annual return in Form FC-4, including a complete audited statement of receipts, the identity of donors, amounts received from each, and a detailed account of how the money was spent. These returns are to be filed on the government's online FCRA portal at https://fcraonline.nic.in/ creating a searchable, annually updated database.

Q. What activities can foreign contributions be used for under FCRA?

A wide range of activities across every sector of Indian society is eligible for foreign funding. These include:

  • Education - schools, colleges, vocational training, scholarship support, adult literacy
  • Healthcare - hospitals, clinics, mobile health units, maternal and child healthcare
  • Rural Development - watershed development, livelihood support, sanitation, clean water access
  • Social Welfare - support for Divyang Jan (persons with disabilities), elderly care, child welfare, women's empowerment
  • Environment - Conservation, afforestation, clean energy, pollution control
  • Culture and Heritage - Preservation of cultural heritage, folk arts, museums
  • Relief and Rehabilitation - Disaster relief, emergency response, post-disaster rehabilitation
  • Faith-Based Welfare - Maintenance of places of worship, religious education, meditation programmes
  • Scientific Research - Research institutions, academic collaborations, knowledge dissemination.

Q. Who cannot receive foreign contributions under FCRA?

A small, fixed list of individuals and entities cannot receive foreign contributions under any circumstances. This list has remained essentially unchanged since 1976 and includes candidates for election, members of legislatures, judges, public servants, political parties and their office-bearers, organisations of a political nature, and specified persons or entities connected with newspapers, news and current-affairs media. The complete statutory list is contained in Section 3 of the Act.

The rationale is straightforward: These categories carry specific responsibilities to India's constitutional institutions that make the receipt of foreign funds a matter of particular sensitivity. The 2020 amendment also extended this restriction to "public servants".

Q. What are the key changes introduced by the FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026 and the revised Rules?

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 (introduced in Lok Sabha on 25 March 2026) and revised FCRA Rules (notified on 22 June 2026) address operational gaps in a governance-focused manner.

Key changes proposed in the 2026 Bill include:

  • Provisional vesting of assets (with full restoration if registration is renewed), similar to the existing provisions under Section 15 of FCRA, 2010.
  • Permanent vesting of assets if NGO does not get its registration restored in prescribed period. (New provision)
  • Right of revision and judicial appeal to the district judge against any order of the designated authority. (New provision)
  • Rationalised penalties (maximum imprisonment reduced from five years to one year)
  • Coordinated investigations (state agencies must obtain central government approval before initiating FCRA probes)

Key changes notified in the 2026 Amendment Rules include:

  • Registration must now name the exact purpose(s) and the State(s)/UT(s) of operation on the certificate, chosen from a prescribed Schedule rather than a broad category.
  • Permissible religious purposes are now explicitly listed in the rules, providing clarity for faith-based organisations across all communities.
  • A requirement that NGOs renewing registration demonstrate utilisation of at least Rs. 10 lakh of FC over the prior two years
  • Enhanced annual reporting with project-wise, activity-wise, and ultimate-donor disclosure, disclosure of the organisation's website and social media.

Q. When was the concept of vesting of assets created out of foreign contribution first introduced?

The concept of vesting of assets created out of foreign contribution upon cancellation was introduced for the first time in 2010 in the original FCRA Act of 2010. As per Section 15 of the existing Act, the assets created from FC shall vest in the Prescribed Authority upon cancellation of FCRA registration. However, if the association subsequently obtains fresh registration, such foreign contribution and assets are required to be returned to it in accordance with law. The prescribed authority is the concerned State Government or Union Territory Administration.

Over the last decade, nearly 22,000 registrations have been cancelled and about 15,000 registrations have been deemed to have ceased, involving foreign contribution and assets worth thousands of crores of rupees. In practice, however, State authorities have faced difficulties in taking possession of, maintaining and managing such assets under the limited framework of the existing Section 15.

The provisions of Section 15 do not comprehensively address all the issues involved. A large number of issues have been left unanswered in the existing provisions. Further, under the existing arrangement, such assets may remain in custodial holding for an indefinite period, without any legal finality. It is neither feasible nor desirable for the Government to preserve and manage such assets indefinitely merely because an association may seek fresh registration at some distant point in the future.

The proposed amendments therefore seek to provide a clear and time-bound framework for provisional vesting, restoration and, where restoration does not take place within the prescribed period, permanent vesting and lawful disposal.

Q. What is the role of the Designated Authority introduced by the 2026 Amendment?

When registration ends, whether through cancellation, surrender, or non-renewal, assets vest provisionally in the Designated Authority. If the organisation successfully gets its registration restored within the prescribed period, all assets and unused funds are returned in full. Only if the organisation does not get its registration restored within the prescribed period do the assets vest permanently, and even then, they are applied towards public purposes by transfer to government department like schools to the Education Department or hospitals to the Health Department. Only in cases where the assets cannot be directly used for public purposes, it will be disposed of with sale proceeds credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. No official benefits personally.

The Designated Authority is also explicitly required by law to preserve the religious character of any place of worship, it cannot convert, repurpose, or secularise a religious institution.

Q. Under the proposed Bill, what happens to an organisation's assets if its FCRA registration is cancelled?

The cancellation of FCRA registration does not mean an organisation's entire assets are seized by the government. The Designated Authority (under the proposed 2026 Amendment) manages only assets created from foreign contributions, and only once an organisation's registration has lawfully ceased.

The process is: upon cancellation, the assets vest provisionally in the Designated Authority; if the organisation gets its registration restored within the prescribed period, all assets and unused funds are returned in full; only if registration is not restored do assets vest permanently; even then, they are applied towards public purposes, and no official benefits personally.

Places of worship retain their religious character by law in all cases. Every order of the Designated Authority is subject to revision within 90 days and further judicial appeal to the District Judge.

Q. Does cessation/ expiry of FCRA registration always mean wrongdoing?

No. The ending of an FCRA registration can occur in different ways. A certificate may expire if renewal is not obtained; an association may surrender it; renewal may be refused; or the registration may be cancelled by a reasoned order on one or more statutory grounds after following the prescribed process. Such expiry should, therefore, not automatically be equated with fraud or criminal wrongdoing. Statutory remedies and constitutional judicial review remain available in accordance with law.

The 2026 Amendment's introduction of automatic cessation (under Section 14B) for registrations not renewed before expiry actually brings clarity and removes earlier administrative ambiguity about the legal status of such organisations. There is no change in the substantive position [Refer Rule 10(1), 12(5) and 12(6)]. The Government’s decision to not renew the registration can be challenged in Courts and is fully under judicial review.

Q. Why does the 2026 Amendment require Central Government approval before state-level FCRA investigations?

FCRA is a central law dealing with foreign relations and national security, both subjects within Parliament's exclusive legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.

Requiring Central Government approval before state agencies initiate FCRA investigations prevents parallel or contradictory proceedings under a single central framework and ensures coordinated, consistent enforcement.

This is consistent with similar provisions in other central laws. It does not limit a state's investigative powers under state laws; it only coordinates investigations under this specific central statute.

Q. What changes have been made regarding the purposes and geographical areas of operation?

Registration certificates will specify the purpose or purposes and the State or Union Territory for which registration is granted, based on the notified list of activities. Existing registered associations have been given one year to furnish this information through Form FC-6F and are not required to seek fresh registration merely for this purpose.

An association that subsequently wishes to add or change an approved purpose or geographical area may apply through the prescribed online process. The objective is to give associations greater clarity regarding their permitted scope of work and to enable activity- and location-based monitoring.

Existing registered associations are not required to apply afresh merely because certificates will now specify purposes and States/UTs. They have been provided with a transition period of one year to furnish the prescribed particulars through Form FC-6F.

Q. Does FCRA target any particular religion or community?

No. The Act applies uniformly to all organisations regardless of religion, community or ideology. Faith-based welfare activities, including religious education, maintenance of places of worship, and charitable work by organisations of every faith, continue to be eligible for foreign funding.

The 2026 Rules have in fact explicitly listed permissible religious purposes, providing greater clarity for faith-based organisations across all communities about the activities eligible for foreign funding.

The restriction on proselytisation introduced by the 2026 Amendment applies equally across all faiths and is consistent with FCRA's longstanding principle that foreign contributions should not be used to alter India's social and demographic fabric through conversion-oriented activity [Refer Sec. 12(4)(a)(ii)].

Q. What is the minimum utilisation requirement introduced for FCRA renewal in 2026?

Under the FCRA amendment Rules of 2026, NGOs renewing FCRA registration must demonstrate that they have utilised at least Rs 10 lakh in foreign contributions over the prior two-year period. This requirement ensures that live FCRA registrations correspond to active, functioning organisations. It prevents dormant entities from holding registrations and retaining the legal ability to receive foreign funds without undertaking any declared activity. [Refer Sec. 12(4)(b) and 14(1)(e)]

Ministry estimates have placed FCRA-registered associations at under 1% of all NGOs operating in India, the law targets a specific, foreign-funded channel, not civil society at large.

Q. Is India an outlier in regulating foreign contributions? How does FCRA compare internationally?

India is not an outlier. Regulating foreign contributions and foreign influence is an established, global practice across leading democracies.

The United States has run the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) since 1938. Australia enacted its Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme in 2018. The United Kingdom's Foreign Influence Registration Scheme under the National Security Act 2023 came into force in July 2025. Canada enacted its Foreign Influence Transparency and Accountability Act in 2024. The European Union is now legislating a comparable directive across all 27 member states.

What they demonstrate is a common democratic principle: foreign funding, direction or influence affecting domestic institutions and public processes may legitimately be made subject to disclosure, accountability and enforcement safeguards.

Q. Is the global trend moving toward more or less foreign influence regulation?

The direction of global trend is clearly towards more foreign-influence regulation, not less — and this has accelerated in the very years FCRA has drawn criticism. The UK's scheme only came into force in July 2025. Canada's registry was legislated in 2024 and is still being implemented.

The EU's proposal followed a Eurobarameter survey in which 81% of Europeans called covert foreign interference a serious problem. Canada's own law records in its preamble a "growing consensus in Canada and among its allies that foreign influence registries are a necessary tool to lessen foreign interference in the affairs of sovereign states." The United States, the original author of this model, has in 2025 directed federal agencies to enforce its 87-year-old FARA more assertively, not less. India has maintained a comparable framework since 1976.

Q. How does the 2026 Amendment strengthen reporting and donor transparency?

The 2026 amendments significantly enhance the quality and depth of annual disclosures. Annual returns will now include project-wise and activity-wise utilisation details (not just aggregate figures), disclosure of the organisation's website and social media handles, and full identification of the ultimate foreign donor even when funds arrive through intermediary channels. This last requirement addresses a specific gap, where the immediate sender of funds was a known entity, but the original foreign source was obscured through multi-layered routing.  The enhanced reporting requirements strengthen the traceability of foreign contributions from their source to their on-ground use.

Transparency in foreign funding is not an obstacle to doing good work. It is the foundation on which trust in that work is built.

 

References:

  • https://fcraonline.gov.in/
  • https://fcraonline.nic.in/home/PDF_Doc/fc_faq_04102022.pdf
  • https://fcraonline.gov.in/legal-framework

2287841.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
Record Scholarship Disbursements Reflect Government's Commitment to Educational Empowerment of Scheduled Caste Students: MoS for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri Ramdas Athawale in Written Reply in Lok Sabha
Post-Matric Scholarship Scheme Benefits Over 48 Lakh SC Students with central assistance amounting to ₹5,562.23 Crores
Pre-Matric Scholarship Scheme Benefits Over 26 Lakh SC Students.With Central Assistance Amounting To ₹562.36 Crore
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:57PM by PIB Delhi

The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is implementing the Post-Matric Scholarship (PMS) Scheme and the Pre-Matric Scholarship Scheme for SCs and Others to provide financial assistance to Scheduled Caste (SC) students pursuing education at various levels. These centrally sponsored scholarship schemes aim to promote educational inclusion, reduce financial barriers and ensure that deserving students are able to continue their studies with adequate financial support.

This information was given by Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri Ramdas Athawale in a written reply to Member of Parliament Shri Navaskani K in Lok Sabha.

The Minister informed the House that the Post-Matric Scholarship Scheme was revised during 2020-21, while the Pre-Matric Scholarship Scheme for SCs and Others was revised in 2021-22. To ensure transparent, efficient and timely delivery of scholarship assistance, the Government has adopted the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) mechanism, under which scholarship amounts are credited directly into the Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts of eligible beneficiaries, the statement added.

The written reply further stated that the reforms have resulted in a significant increase in financial assistance under the Post-Matric Scholarship Scheme. The Central assistance released under the scheme increased from ₹1,930.38 crores in 2021-22 to ₹6,186.96 crores in 2025-26. The scheme has consistently benefited nearly 48 lakh Scheduled Caste students annually in recent years. During 2024-25, a total of 48,04,208 beneficiaries received scholarships with central assistance amounting to ₹5,562.23 crore.

The Minister further informed the House that under the Pre-Matric Scholarship Scheme for SCs and Others, the Government has continued extending financial support to lakhs of students. During 2025-26, central assistance amounting to   was released, benefiting 26,79,049 students. Since the implementation of the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system under the scheme from 2022-23, scholarship disbursement has become more transparent, accountable and efficient.

The Government continues to strengthen educational opportunities for Scheduled Caste students through enhanced scholarship support and technology-enabled delivery mechanisms. By expanding coverage, increasing financial assistance and ensuring transparent transfer of benefits through DBT, the Ministry remains committed to promoting educational empowerment, social justice and equitable access to quality education for Scheduled Caste students across the country.

2287825.title: ICMR-NIN-led ‘Let’s Fix Our Food’ Consortium Releases Policy Priorities to Promote Healthier Diets for Children and Adolescents
2287825.ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
2287825.body_html:
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
ICMR-NIN-led ‘Let’s Fix Our Food’ Consortium Releases Policy Priorities to Promote Healthier Diets for Children and Adolescents
Policy document outlines evidence-based recommendations to create healthier food environments and improve dietary behaviours among children and adolescents
NITI Aayog Member (Health) Dr. M. Srinivas launches policy document during LFOF Dissemination and Consultation Workshop in New Delhi
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:44PM by PIB Delhi

The Indian Council of Medical Research–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN)-led 'Let's Fix Our Food' (LFOF) Consortium today released a policy document titled 'Priority Policy Actions to Promote Healthier Diets and Food Environments for Children and Adolescents in India', outlining evidence-based recommendations to support healthier food environments and improve dietary behaviours among children and adolescents across the country.

The policy document was launched by Dr. M. Srinivas, Member (Health), NITI Aayog, during the LFOF Dissemination and Consultation Workshop held at the India Habitat Centre, New Delhi, in the presence of Dr. Bharati Kulkarni, Director, ICMR-NIN, Prof. (Dr.) K. Srinath Reddy, Founder President, Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI), and senior representatives from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, FSSAI, UNICEF India, Resolve to Save Lives (RTSL), consortium partner institutions, researchers, development partners and youth representatives.

The Let's Fix Our Food (LFOF) Consortium is a multi-institutional national platform led by ICMR-NIN, with participation from Resolve to Save Lives (RTSL) India, UNICEF India, Global Health Advocacy Incubator (GHAI), PHFI, WHO, FSSAI, IEG, WFP, Lady Irwin College, IFPRI, Deakin University and other national and international partners. Through research, policy analysis, advocacy and stakeholder engagement, the Consortium seeks to support India's efforts to prevent diet-related non-communicable diseases by transforming food environments, particularly for children and adolescents.

The publication brings together nearly three years of multidisciplinary research, stakeholder consultations and policy dialogues. It sets out policy recommendations across key areas, including healthy school food environments, nutrition literacy, front-of-pack nutrition labelling, regulation of marketing of unhealthy food to children, taxation of foods high in fat, salt and sugar (HFSS), healthier dietary fats, salt reduction, low-sodium salt substitutes, social and behaviour change communication, youth engagement and fiscal measures to promote healthier diets.

Speaking on the occasion, Dr. M. Srinivas, Member (Health), NITI Aayog, said, "Evidence-based, multisectoral policy action is essential to create healthier food environments for children and adolescents. Collaborative initiatives such as the Let's Fix Our Food Consortium are important for addressing the growing burden of overweight, obesity and diet-related non-communicable diseases in India."

Dr. Bharati Kulkarni, Director, ICMR-NIN, said, "ICMR-NIN is committed to generating high-quality evidence and fostering partnerships that translate research into public health action. The policy recommendations reflect the collective efforts of researchers, policymakers, development partners and young people working towards healthier food environments for India's future generations."

Prof. (Dr.) K. Srinath Reddy, Founder President, Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI), underscored the need for comprehensive policy interventions addressing the commercial, social and environmental determinants of unhealthy diets, and called for sustained action to protect children and adolescents from obesogenic food environments.

The workshop also witnessed the launch of several knowledge products developed under the Consortium, including the LFOF website, the Nutrition Environment Assessment Toolkit for Schools (NEAT-S) and its report, an e-learning module on understanding food labels, and a suite of ICMR-NIN educational resources on fats, sugars and salt to strengthen nutrition literacy among children and adolescents.

Marie-Claude Desilets, Chief of Nutrition, UNICEF India, said, "Malnutrition is no longer only about undernutrition. Rising obesity, driven by unhealthy diets, challenges healthy growth among children and adolescents. The release of these ten policy briefs and the Nutrition Environment Assessment Toolkit for Schools (NEAT-S) marks a step towards creating policies for healthier school food environments. Every child has the right to grow up in a food environment that enables them to thrive, learn and achieve their full potential."

Dr. Syed Imran Farooq, Executive Director, Resolve to Save Lives (RTSL), highlighted the need to reduce excess salt, fat and sugar intake alongside food policies that support healthier food environments and lower the burden of cardiovascular diseases and other health threats. He also acknowledged the leadership of ICMR-NIN and reaffirmed RTSL's commitment to the shared vision of healthier food environments across India.

The consultation showcased new evidence generated by consortium partners on school food environments, unhealthy food marketing, nutrition education, dietary behaviours, fiscal policy options and nutrition environment assessments across multiple states. The workshop concluded with thematic discussions on translating evidence into actionable policy recommendations to support healthier food environments for children and adolescents.

Background

The Let's Fix Our Food Consortium was established to generate evidence and catalyse policy action for healthier food environments in India, with a special focus on children and adolescents. The policy priorities released today draw on multidisciplinary research and consultations and seek to support efforts to prevent diet-related non-communicable diseases through coordinated, evidence-informed action.

The policy briefs are available at: https://letsfixourfood.org/LFOF-policy-brief.php.

2287817.title: Branch of the Bharatiya Beej Sahakari Samiti Limited in Bihar
2287817.body_html:
Ministry of Cooperation
Branch of the Bharatiya Beej Sahakari Samiti Limited in Bihar
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:38PM by PIB Delhi

No formal branch office of Bharatiya Beej Sahakari Samiti Limited (BBSSL) has presently been established in Bihar. However, BBSSL has an operational presence in the State through its field official, who coordinates seed distribution, business development and monitoring of seed-related activities.

BBSSL is undertaking seed business in Bihar through the Bihar Rajya Beej Nigam Limited, which is the designated nodal agency for BBSSL in the State. Seed production and distribution activities are coordinated with the nodal agency, local cooperative institutions and other stakeholders. During the financial year 2026–27, BBSSL has also supplied various crop seeds directly to 20 cooperative societies in Bihar, thereby strengthening its cooperative-based distribution network in the State.

BBSSL follows a farmer-centric pricing model under which seed-producing farmers are paid the highest of: (i) MSP plus a minimum 10 per cent incentive on graded seed, or (ii) the prevailing mandi market price, or (iii) the concerned State Seed Corporation’s procurement rate. This ensures assured procurement, protects farmers from price fluctuations and provides them a remunerative premium for meeting the higher quality and technical requirements of seed production.

This information was given by Union Minister for Home and Cooperation Shri Amit Shah in a written reply in Rajya Sabha.

2287806.title: Strengthening of cooperative societies in Odisha
2287806.body_html:
Ministry of Cooperation
Strengthening of cooperative societies in Odisha
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:34PM by PIB Delhi

As per the National Cooperative Database (NCD), as on 15.07.2026, there are a total of 8,667 cooperative societies in Odisha, out of which 8,063 cooperative societies are functional.

To strengthen cooperative societies, the Government launched the Central Sector project for Computerization of PACS, in 2022. Initially, 63,000 PACS were approved under the project with a total financial outlay of ₹2,516 crore. The project has now been expanded to cover 79,630 PACS with a revised financial outlay of ₹2,925.39 crore. It aims to bring all functional PACS onto a common ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) based national software. The project also links PACS with NABARD through State Cooperative Banks (StCBs) and District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs). Odisha joined the project in 2025. A total of 4,240 PACS have been sanctioned under the PACS computerization project in Odisha. Under the project, financial assistance of ₹25.07 crore has been provided to Odisha. This includes ₹18.07 crore during FY 2025–26 and ₹7.00 crore during FY 2026–27.

Additionally, as on 30.06.2026, the National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC) has cumulatively disbursed ₹3,352.03 crore for the development of the cooperative sector in Odisha. The year-wise details of the amount disbursed during the last five years are given at Annexure-1.

The Ministry of Cooperation, since its inception on 06.07.2021, has undertaken several initiatives to realize the vision of “Sahakar-se-Samriddhi” and to enhance the cooperative growth across the country including Odisha. Key areas of initiatives include:

  1. Making Primary Cooperatives economically vibrant and transparent;
  2. Strengthening the Urban and Rural Cooperative Banks;
  3. Relief to Cooperative Societies in the Income Tax Act;
  4. Revival of Cooperative Sugar Mills;
  5. Three new National Level Multi-State Societies;
  6. Capacity Building in Cooperatives;
  7. Use of Information Technology for ‘Ease of Doing Business’;
  8. Creation of National Cooperative Database (NCD);
  9. National Cooperation Policy (NCP);
  10. Establishment of Tribhuvan Sahkari University
  11. Other Initiatives

The Ministry of Cooperation has taken proactive measures to convert Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), Dairy, and Fisheries Cooperatives into Multipurpose cooperative societies. This initiative aims to enhance business diversification, strengthen financial sustainability, and prevent closures by enabling cooperatives to engage in a wider range of economic activities. The NCD is used for identification of gaps in the geographical spread of cooperatives, thereby supporting the formation of new multipurpose PACS/dairy/fisheries cooperative societies. It also enables the development of the Cooperative Ranking Framework to promote healthy competition.

Additionally, the Ministry of Cooperation has set up Co-operative Rehabilitation, Reconstruction and Development Fund under section 63A of the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (MSCS) (Amendment) Act, 2023 for revival of sick multi-State cooperative societies and providing assistance for meeting infrastructural requirement.

2287804.title: Status of Bharat Taxi
2287804.body_html:
Ministry of Cooperation
Status of Bharat Taxi
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:33PM by PIB Delhi

Sahakar Taxi Cooperative Limited (STCL), registered under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, 2002, was established on 6 June 2025 by eight national-level cooperative institutions and was officially launched on 5 February 2026 under the aegis of the Ministry of Cooperation. STCL has introduced a cooperative-based mobility ecosystem that represents a paradigm shift from the conventional “driver-partner” model to the “Sarathi-owner” model, under which drivers become members and owners of the cooperative society, participate in its governance through representation on the Board of Management, and share in the cooperative's surplus.

Through its Bharat Taxi platform, STCL operates on a zero-commission model, enabling drivers to retain their earnings while the cooperative's surplus is distributed among its Sarathi-members. The platform integrates cooperative ownership with technology-enabled ride-hailing services, including transparent fare structures, real-time vehicle tracking, multilingual mobile interfaces, and round-the-clock customer support, providing a homegrown and indigenous alternative to investment-driven aggregator platforms.

The implementation of Bharat Taxi Services is being carried out in a phased manner across the country. The Bharat Taxi platform, comprising the Sarathi (driver) application, passenger application and the backend management system, has been developed and is being expanded in a phased manner. The rollout in individual cities and States is contingent on factors such as operational preparedness, availability of Sarathis, completion of statutory requirements, and coordination with the concerned State Governments, cooperative institutions and other stakeholders.

The implementation includes registration and onboarding of Sarathis, customer enrolment, training programmes and expansion of services to identified cities and States.

7.76 lakh Sarathis (drivers) have been registered on the Bharat Taxi platform and their document verification has been completed. 40.84 lakh customers have been registered on the platform. Presently the Bharat Taxi is operational in cities of Delhi-NCR and Gujrat.

Bharat Taxi and Yatri Sathi are separate mobility platforms operating under different institutional arrangements.

Bharat Taxi is a cooperative-based mobility platform operated by STCL under the provisions of the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, 2002. Yatri Sathi is a State Government initiative developed, owned and operated by the Department of Information Technology and Electronics (DITE), Government of West Bengal for providing taxi aggregation services within the State.

This information was given by Union Minister for Home and Cooperation Shri Amit Shah in a written reply in Rajya Sabha.

2287796.title: Promotion of AI and digital platforms in cooperatives
2287796.body_html:
Ministry of Cooperation
Promotion of AI and digital platforms in cooperatives
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:29PM by PIB Delhi

AI and digital platforms are getting progressively promoted across cooperative training institutions through academic, training and institutional initiatives. Technology-driven teaching pedagogy and learning platforms are being adopted by cooperative training institutions such as RICM, Chandigarh in Punjab. The measures include use of smart classrooms with interactive digital boards, projectors and ICT-enabled teaching tools; adoption of blended learning through e-content, online classes and Learning Management Systems (LMS); and training of faculty in ICT tools and digital pedagogy. Digital learning initiatives are also reviewed periodically for their effective utilisation.

Capacity building for teachers and cooperative professionals is being supported through Faculty Development Programmes (FDPs), refresher courses, seminars, workshops, webinars and other professional development programmes. The programmes cover areas such as cooperative management, banking and finance, governance, digital banking, digital transformation and other emerging areas of the cooperative sector.

This information was given by Union Minister for Home and Cooperation Shri Amit Shah in a written reply in Rajya Sabha.

2287792.title: ‘Heritage Artisan Cooperatives’
2287792.body_html:
Ministry of Cooperation
‘Heritage Artisan Cooperatives’
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:25PM by PIB Delhi

Based on the information received from the State of Odisha, Directorate of Handicrafts under the administrative control of Handlooms, Textiles & Handicrafts Department, Odisha, the functioning of Handicraft Cooperative Societies (HCSs) of Odisha including the HCSs of Puri district is supervised time to time. An integrated RCS digital portal has been launched in Odisha. As per the National Cooperative Database (NCD), there are a total of 756 registered cooperative societies in the Puri district.

The National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC) implements sector-specific schemes and focused financial products aligned with the evolving needs of the cooperative sector, including artisan cooperative societies across the country, including those in the Puri district of Odisha. Details of the Schemes of NCDC are enclosed at Annexure A.

The key measures undertaken to support and strengthen this artisan cooperatives are as under:

  • Financial Assistance for Infrastructure & Marketing: NCDC provides financial assistance to eligible artisan cooperatives for infrastructure creation, value addition, processing, and marketing of artisan and handicraft products.
  • Capacity Building & Entrepreneurship: Various training and awareness programmes are regularly conducted for artisans to facilitate entrepreneurship development, marketing support, and to improve their access to institutional finance.
  • Promotion of Digital Literacy: To facilitate digital onboarding and modern business practices, digital literacy is integrated as an essential component of all training and capacity-building interventions.

These promotional and financial assistance schemes are available to all eligible artisan cooperative societies across the country, including Puri, subject to the fulfilment of the prescribed guidelines and eligibility criteria under the respective schemes. These provide opportunity to address and overcome, challenges.

As on 30.06.2026, NCDC has disbursed ₹ 3,352.03 crore for cooperative development in Odisha State. The details of disbursement during last five years in the State is provided at Annexure-B. As on 30.06.2026, NCDC has disbursed ₹3.78 Cr in Puri district during the last five years (since 01.04.2021). There are 17 HCSs functional in Puri district which are engaged in different handicrafts. Other artisans are sensitized on digital literacy and consolidation of required documents for their onboarding into e-commerce platforms through different training programmes and awareness camps.   Marketing assistance to handicraft artisans/ members of Handicrafts Cooperative Societies is provided through exhibitions/ fairs/ melas organized at District level/ State level and National level.

******

It converges critical inputs of women’s enterprise, business plan formulation, capacity development, credit and subsidy, and/ or interest subvention of other schemes.

DAIRY SAHAKAR: The scheme launched in the financial year 2021-22 is a cooperative dairy business focused framework of financial assistance for encouraging cooperatives to achieve higher outcomes in ESG (environmental, social, governance) linked activities. It includes the creation of infrastructure by cooperatives for new projects and modernization and/or expansion of existing projects.

 

  1. 2287789.title: Review of National Cooperation Policy, 2025
2287789.body_html:
Ministry of Cooperation
Review of National Cooperation Policy, 2025
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:23PM by PIB Delhi

A national-level ‘Policy Implementation and Monitoring Committee’ has been established with a mandate of central-state coordination, troubleshooting implementation bottlenecks, periodic monitoring and evaluation, etc. The ‘Policy Implementation and Monitoring Committee’ held its first meeting on 09.06.2026, the members of the Committee were from Central Ministries/Departments, National Federations/National Cooperative Societies, and representatives and senior officials from State Governments. In its first meeting, it was informed that the NCP was implemented through the Whole-of-Government approach and in the spirit of cooperative federalism.

        The institutional mechanism for monitoring the implementation of the policy given in   NCP 2025 are as follows:

“9.5.1. A ‘National Steering Committee on Cooperation Policy’, chaired by the Union Minister of Cooperation, to be constituted for overall guidance, inter-ministerial coordination, periodic policy review, etc. This committee may include the Hon’ble Minister-in-charge of related Ministries of the Government of India as members,

9.5.2. A national-level ‘Policy Implementation and Monitoring Committee’, chaired by the Union Cooperation Secretary, to be established for central-state coordination, troubleshooting implementation bottlenecks, periodic monitoring and evaluation, etc. It may comprise members, including the Secretary of related Ministries of the Government of India, Secretaries/Principal Secretaries/Additional Chief Secretaries of the Cooperative Department of all States/Union Territories, a representative from NITI Aayog, and Chairpersons/MDs of national cooperative federations/unions/societies, NABARD, NDDB, NCDC, NFDB, NCCT, VAMNICOM, etc.”

 

          Both the above committees have been constituted.

The policy provides a roadmap for the systematic and holistic development of the cooperative sector. It has 6 strategic pillars, 16 objectives, and 83 recommendations. The Policy enunciates a vision, a mission, and 16 specific objectives to be achieved over the next 10 years.

      A comprehensive National Cooperative Database (NCD) has been developed by the Ministry of Cooperation with the support of States / UTs. This database provides a single-point access to information on over 8.5 lakh cooperatives societies across 30 economic sectors, having approximately 30 crore members. The data of the Cooperative Societies is collected and updated regularly on the NCD portal by nodal officers appointed by the States/ UTs for this purpose. The State-wise details of cooperative societies across the country are attached as Annexure-A.

      The NCD plays an important role not only during the formulation of any policy intervention but during policy implementation as well. The database provides critical insights into cooperatives’ geographical coverage, financial performance, etc., and thereby helps implement the policy recommendations. The database serves as an important tool for formation of new PACS, dairy and fisheries primary cooperatives in uncovered and under-covered areas, enables development of a ranking framework, and assists in estimating the economic contribution of cooperative sector in the Indian economy.

2287788.title: INDIAN NAVY COMMISSIONS INS MALVAN, THE SECOND OF THE MAHE-CLASS ANTI-SUBMARINE WARFARE SHALLOW WATER CRAFT
2287788.body_html:
Ministry of Defence
INDIAN NAVY COMMISSIONS INS MALVAN, THE SECOND OF THE MAHE-CLASS ANTI-SUBMARINE WARFARE SHALLOW WATER CRAFT
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:21PM by PIB Delhi

INS Malvan, the second of the indigenously designed and built Mahe-class Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft (ASW-SWC), was commissioned at Karwar on 22 Jul 2026. The event was presided over by Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, Chief of the Air Staff, in the presence of Vice Admiral Sanjay Vatsayan, Flag Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Western Naval Command. Other senior naval officers, representatives from Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL), Kochi, veterans, and distinguished guests were also in attendance.

The ship carries deep historical and cultural significance as it derives its name from the historical coastal town of Malvan in Maharashtra, a region intrinsically linked to the illustrious maritime heritage of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj. The vessel also encapsulates the legacy of her predecessor, an inshore Indian Naval Minesweeper that remained in service till 2003.

INS Malvan is the second of eight ASW-SWCs, being indigenously built by CSL, Kochi, and the sixth of 16 ASW-SWCs to be commissioned into Indian Navy. With over 80 percent indigenous content, the ship reinforces the Government of India’s vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat and India’s expanding ecosystem of naval design, equipment, system integration, and growing self-reliance in defence shipbuilding.

The vessel is equipped for Underwater Surveillance, Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) operations, and Low Intensity Maritime Operations (LIMO) along with Mine Warfare capability. The vessel will further bolster coastal defence, littoral security, and enhance Maritime Domain Awareness.

The crest of INS Malvan carries the ‘Bagh Nakha’ (Tiger's Claw), symbolising bravery, warfare tactics, agility, and audacity, resonating with the ship's ethos to attack rapidly and strike silently. The waves surrounding ‘Bagh Nakha’ reflect the vast sea surrounding the coasts and the Indian Navy's unwavering resolve to remain ever vigilant, ever ready, and steadfast in safeguarding the nation's seas and sovereignty. The ship's motto, ‘Silent Claws’, embodies lethality, stealth, and the ability to strike the adversary swiftly.

Addressing the gathering on the occasion, the Chief of the Air Staff emphasised the critical importance of safeguarding sea lines of communication to ensure unimpeded maritime trade amid global uncertainties. He lauded the Indian Navy's impressive growth and its commitment to the Aatmanirbhar initiative, specifically highlighting the warship's over 80 percent indigenous content. Drawing inspiration from the Indian Navy's model of embedding officers directly into the shipbuilding process, he suggested that similar practices could accelerate self-reliance across the broader defence ecosystem. He also reaffirmed the vision of tri-service integration, calling for seamless jointness among the Indian Army, Indian Navy, and Indian Air Force to ensure the nation succeeds as one unified force in future conflicts.

The commissioning of INS Malvan adds a significant punch to the Indian Navy’s Anti-Submarine Warfare capabilities. With the ability to operate seamlessly with larger surface combatants, submarines, and aviation assets, induction of INS Malvan enables the Indian Navy to remain Combat Ready, Credible, Cohesive, and Future Ready to ensure national security and safeguard India’s maritime interests at all times and at all locations.

2287784.title: Cooperative societies in Maharashtra
2287784.body_html:
Ministry of Cooperation
Cooperative societies in Maharashtra
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:18PM by PIB Delhi

As per the National Cooperative Database (NCD), as on 15.07.2026, there are a total of 2,27,177 cooperative societies in Maharashtra. The sector-wise details of total number of cooperative societies, district federations and state federations in Maharashtra, are attached as Annexure-1.

The Government launched the Central Sector project for Computerization of PACS, in 2022. Initially, 63,000 PACS were approved under the project with a total financial outlay of ₹2,516 crore. The project has now been expanded to cover 79,630 PACS with a revised financial outlay of ₹2,925.39 crore. It aims to bring all functional PACS onto a common ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) based national software. The project also links PACS with NABARD through State Cooperative Banks (StCBs) and District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs). A total of 12,178 PACS have been sanctioned under the PACS computerization project in Maharashtra. Under the project, financial assistance of ₹29.14 crore has been provided to Maharashtra. This includes ₹9.14 crore during in FY 2025–26, and ₹20.00 crore in FY 2026–27.

Additionally, as on 30.06.2026, NCDC has cumulatively disbursed ₹34,161.54 crore for the development of cooperative sector in Maharashtra. The year-wise details of the amount disbursed during the last five years are given at Annexure-1.

The Ministry of Cooperation, since its inception on 06.07.2021, has undertaken several initiatives to realize the vision of “Sahakar-se-Samriddhi” and to strengthen dairy, sugar and agri-cooperatives across the country including Maharashtra. These initiatives include:

I. Model Bye-laws for PACS: Enabled PACS to undertake more than 25 business activities, improve governance, transparency and accountability in their operations. Now, PACS can operate as PM-Kisan Samridhi Kendras (PMKSKs), Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Kendras (PMBJKs), Common Service Centres (CSC) etc.

II. Cooperative-led White Revolution 2.0: Aims to increase milk procurement by dairy cooperatives by 50% over five years. It also focuses on expanding cooperative coverage, generating employment and promoting women’s empowerment.

III. Income Tax Relief: Clarified that cooperative sugar mills are not liable to additional income tax on higher sugarcane prices paid up to Fair and Remunerative or State Advised Price, with effect from April 2016.

IV. Tax Relief in Union Budget 2023–24: Allowed sugar cooperatives to claim payments made to sugarcane farmers before AY 2016–17 as expenditure, providing relief of over ₹46,000 crore.

V. Financial Support through NCDC: Launched a scheme for ethanol plants, cogeneration plants and working capital. The Ministry released ₹1,000 crore to NCDC, which has disbursed ₹10,005 crore to 56 cooperative sugar mills.

VI. Ethanol Blending Programme: Brought cooperative sugar mills at par with private companies for ethanol procurement under the EBP.

VII. Reduction in GST on Molasses: Reduced GST on molasses from 28% to 5%, increasing margins and profits for cooperative sugar mills.

VIII. Revival of Closed Sugar Mills: Indian Potash Limited has taken an initiative to revive closed cooperative sugar mills on the suggestion of the Ministry of Cooperation.

2287778.title: Comprehensive Infrastructure and Welfare Initiatives Strengthen Haj Management for Indian Pilgrims
2287778.body_html:
Ministry of Minority Affairs
Comprehensive Infrastructure and Welfare Initiatives Strengthen Haj Management for Indian Pilgrims
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:16PM by PIB Delhi

The Government, through the Ministry of Minority Affairs and the Haj Committee of India, in coordination with the concerned authorities in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, has undertaken various initiatives to modernise and enhance the infrastructure and facilities for Indian Haj pilgrims. Some of the major initiatives are as follows:

  1. Improved Infrastructure at Mina Camps: The traditional accommodation arrangements at Mina have been upgraded by providing sofa-cum-beds, ensuring greater comfort, better utilisation of available space and improved living conditions for pilgrims during their stay.
  2. High-Speed Train Connectivity: Indian Haj pilgrims are facilitated to travel between Makkah and Madinah through the High-Speed Rail, which has significantly reduced travel time, improved safety, and enhanced overall travel convenience.
  3. Haj Suvidha App: The Ministry has developed the Haj Suvidha App, a comprehensive digital platform that enables pilgrims to access important Haj-related services such as travel details, accommodation information, baggage tracking, emergency contacts, grievance redressal, health-related information, and other essential services, thereby improving communication and service delivery throughout the pilgrimage.
  4. Hotel-Style Accommodation in Makkah: Hotel-style accommodation has been arranged for Indian Haj pilgrims in Makkah with improved amenities and services, ensuring enhanced comfort, better accessibility, and a more convenient stay during the Haj period.

 The Government has undertaken several measures to improve coordination between the Ministry, the Haj Committee of India, and State Haj Committees for the preparations for Haj-2026. These include strengthened institutional coordination through periodic review meetings, issuance of detailed guidelines and timelines for all operational activities, and regular consultations to streamline accommodation, transport, training, and other logistical arrangements.

The allocation of Haj quota among States and Union Territories is made in proportion to their Muslim population as per the latest applicable Census data. Accordingly, there is no separate proposal under consideration for increasing the Haj quota of the State of Tamil Nadu.

The Government has taken several initiatives to ensure the safety, comfort and logistical convenience of Haj pilgrims, with special emphasis on senior citizens and first-time pilgrims. The major initiatives are as follows:

  1. Mandatory Companion for Elderly Pilgrims: Pilgrims aged 65 years and above are required to be accompanied by a companion to ensure adequate assistance and support throughout the pilgrimage.
  2. Comprehensive Insurance Coverage: Every Haj pilgrim is provided with insurance coverage of up to ₹6.25 lakh, offering financial protection in the event of unforeseen contingencies during the Haj journey.
  3. SHI Ratio: For Haj 2026, the State Haj Inspector ratio has been improved to 1:150, ensuring better accessibility and prompt services for pilgrims.
  4. Pre-Departure Training: All selected Haj pilgrims are imparted comprehensive orientation and training before their departure to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, covering pilgrimage rituals, travel procedures, health advisories, safety measures, and the use of digital services.
  5. Medical Infrastructure in Saudi Arabia: Medical infrastructure comprising hospitals, medical centres and dispensaries is established at key pilgrimage locations in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to provide timely and quality healthcare services during the Haj period. The Government deputes qualified doctors, paramedics and other medical personnel to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to provide medical assistance and emergency healthcare services to Indian Haj pilgrims.

These initiatives collectively aim to provide a safer, more comfortable and pilgrim-friendly Haj experience, particularly for senior citizens and first-time Haj travellers.

This information was given by Union Minister of Minority Affairs Shri Kiren Rijiju in a written reply in Rajya Sabha today.

2287777.title: Government Enhances Digital Governance and Pilgrim Welfare for Haj 2026
2287777.body_html:
Ministry of Minority Affairs
Government Enhances Digital Governance and Pilgrim Welfare for Haj 2026
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:15PM by PIB Delhi

The Government has undertaken several digital initiatives to improve the management of the Haj pilgrimage for Indian pilgrims during Haj 2026. The major initiatives are as follows:

  1. Haj Suvidha App 2.0: The Ministry has launched Haj Suvidha App 2.0, an enhanced digital platform providing pilgrims with end-to-end information and services relating to their Haj journey. The App facilitates access to travel schedules, accommodation details, baggage information, emergency contacts, SOS, health-related information, important advisories, and grievance redressal, thereby improving communication and service delivery. Pilgrims can register and track grievances through the Haj Suvidha App, facilitating timely resolution and improved service delivery.
  2. Online Haj Application and Selection: The Haj application process is conducted through an online portal & Haj Suvidha App, and the selection of pilgrims is carried out through a transparent, computerised process, ensuring efficiency and transparency.
  3. Online Payment System: Pilgrims can make Haj-related payments through secure online payment modes, facilitating timely and convenient financial transactions.
  4. Online Flight Selection: Pilgrims are provided with the facility to indicate their preferred flight dates and timings through the online system, subject to operational feasibility, thereby improving convenience and travel planning.
  5. Digital Submission of Passports: The requirement for physical submission of passports has been dispensed with. Pilgrims can submit passport details digitally, reducing paperwork, processing time and the need for repeated visits to State/UT Haj Committees.
  6. Digital Accommodation and Pilgrim Information: Details relating to accommodation, flight details and other pilgrim-specific services are made available digitally through the Haj Suvidha App and the online Haj portal, enabling pilgrims to access information conveniently.

The Government has taken several measures to enhance the welfare of Indian Haj pilgrims during Haj 2026, particularly in the areas of healthcare, accommodation, transportation and emergency assistance. The major initiatives are as follows:

  1. Improved Accommodation: Hotel-style accommodation has been arranged for Indian Haj pilgrims in Makkah for Haj-2026 with improved amenities and services. In Mina camps, the traditional accommodation arrangements have been upgraded by providing sofa-cum-beds, ensuring greater comfort and better utilisation of space.
  2. Medical Infrastructure in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia: Clinics, medical centres and dispensaries are established at key pilgrimage locations to provide medical services to Indian Haj pilgrims throughout the Haj period. The Government deputes qualified doctors, paramedics and other medical personnel to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to provide medical assistance to Indian Haj pilgrims.
  3. Comprehensive Insurance Coverage: Every Haj pilgrim is covered under a comprehensive insurance scheme providing coverage of up to ₹6.25 lakh, offering financial protection against unforeseen contingencies during the pilgrimage.
  4. Improved Transportation: Indian Haj pilgrims are facilitated to travel between Makkah and Madinah through the High-Speed Rail, significantly reducing travel time and enhancing safety and convenience.
  5. Special Facilitation for Vulnerable Pilgrims: Pilgrims aged 65 years and above are required to be accompanied by a companion to ensure adequate support and assistance throughout the pilgrimage.

The Government is committed to ensure the safety, welfare, comfort and overall well-being of Indian Haj pilgrims through digital services and reforms.

This information was given by Union Minister of Minority Affairs Shri Kiren Rijiju in a written reply in Rajya Sabha today.

2287773.title: National Commission for Minorities Promotes Dialogue and Inclusive Development through National Outreach Initiatives
2287773.body_html:
Ministry of Minority Affairs
National Commission for Minorities Promotes Dialogue and Inclusive Development through National Outreach Initiatives
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 5:14PM by PIB Delhi

The details of seminars and conference organised by National Commission for Minorities (NCM) are at Annexure.

NCM has conducted a study on the subject “Contribution of Jain Community in the Field of Education” during 2026. The study documents the historical evolution, institutional contribution and educational philosophy of the Jain community in India. It captures the role of Jain trusts, philanthropists, educational institutions and community organisations in promoting learning, research, scholarships, value-based education and inclusive access to education.

National Commission for Minorities (NCM), in discharge of its advisory and facilitative mandate, organized Conference of State Minorities Commissions on the 19th May 2026 at New Delhi, which was attended by representatives of State Minorities Commissions, including the Maharashtra State Minorities Commission, along with officials of State Governments and Union Territories. The Conference served as a platform to deliberate on institutional strengthening,
administrative coordination, grievance redressal mechanisms, and the exchange of best practices for enhancing outreach and improving the delivery of welfare measures for minority communities.

The Commission also organized a series of national seminars on the Buddhist, Jain and Parsi communities during 2026 to facilitate dialogue, research and awareness on issues concerning minority communities and to encourage greater dissemination of information on Government welfare initiatives. During these events, the Government's commitment towards the welfare and inclusive development of minority communities was highlighted alongwith various welfare initiatives and programmes.  

****

Annexure

Details of the seminars, conference and outreach progammes organized by National Commission for Minorities during 2026                                                  

  1. National Seminar on "Buddhism in Modern India: Navigating Cultural and Social Pathways" (27.02.2026, New Delhi)

The National Commission for Minorities (NCM) organized a National seminar on “Buddhism in Modern India: Navigating Cultural and Social Pathways” on 27.02.2026 in New Delhi. The Seminar was graced by Hon’ble Minister of Minority Affairs, and Hon’ble Minister of State for Minority Affairs. The seminar focused on heritage preservation, education, youth engagement and the role of Buddhist philosophy in promoting peace and social harmony. The seminar brought together policymakers, scholars, spiritual leaders, and community representatives to deliberate on the evolving role of Buddhism in India’s socio-cultural landscape.


  1. National Seminar on "The Contribution of the Jain Community to the Indian Economy, Education and Philanthropy" (23.04.2026, Indore)

National Commission for Minorities (NCM), in collaboration with Devi Ahilya Vishwavidyalaya (DAVV), Indore, organized a National Seminar on “The Contribution of the Jain Community to the Indian Economy, Education, and Philanthropy” on 23.4.20226 in Indore. The Seminar was graced by Hon’ble Minister of State for Minority Affairs. The seminar brought together scholars, academicians, industrialists, philanthropists, students, and members of the Jain community to discuss the community’s significant role in nation-building.


  1. National Seminar on "Parsis in Modern India: Navigating Cultural and Socio-Economic Pathways" (09.05.2026, Mumbai)

National Commission for Minorities (NCM) organized a National Seminar on “Parsis in Modern India: Navigating Cultural and Socio-Economic Pathways” on 09.05.2026 in Mumbai. The Seminar was graced by Hon’ble Minister of Minority Affairs, and Hon’ble Minister of State for Minority Affairs. The seminar focused on the preservation of Parsi heritage, socio-economic development, demographic challenges and the community's invaluable contribution to nation-building. The seminar brought together ministers, policymakers, scholars, industrialists, academicians, and members of the Parsi community to discuss issues related to cultural preservation, demographic challenges, and socio-economic development.


  1. Conference of State Minorities Commissions (19.05.2026, New Delhi)

National Commission for Minorities organized the Conference of State Minorities Commissions on 19th May 2026 at New Delhi to discuss minority welfare, protection of minority rights and inclusive development. The Seminar was graced by Hon’ble Minister of Minority Affairs, and Hon’ble Minister of State for Minority Affairs. The Conference deliberated on best practices, challenges faced by State Commissions and the role of minority communities in nation-building. The conference brought together representatives from State Minorities Commissions, State Governments, Union Territories and minority communities to strengthen coordination and welfare mechanisms across the country.

This information was given by Union Minister of Minority Affairs Shri Kiren Rijiju in a written reply in Rajya Sabha today.

Radhakrishnan, today called for strengthening India’s healthcare ecosystem through a skilled, compassionate and service-oriented workforce, saying that quality healthcare and education are the twin pillars of a healthy and developed nation. Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan inaugurated the GKNM college of Nursing in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu today.

Emphasising the vital role of nurses, the Vice President said they are far more than caregivers - they instill confidence, comfort and hope in patients, with their… pic.twitter.com/dGWcWVDx1N

— Vice-President of India (@VPIndia) July 22, 2026

Addressing the gathering after inaugurating the GKNM Group College of Nursing in Coimbatore, the Vice-President described the institution as another milestone in the long tradition of public service rendered by the GKNM Group. He commended the G. Kuppuswamy Naidu Charitable Trust for its remarkable contribution to healthcare and education over the past several decades, noting that its 50-bed hospital established in 1952 has today grown into a 750-bed multi-specialty institution while simultaneously expanding its educational initiatives from schools to higher education.

Emphasising the importance of the nursing profession, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan said nurses are far more than caregivers. “They make patients feel safe, secure and cared for. Along with medicines, their compassion and concern play an indispensable role in healing,” he said. He urged students entering the profession to carry out their responsibilities with self-confidence, compassion, dedication and courage, and always uphold the nobility of their calling.

Highlighting the transformation taking place in India’s healthcare sector, the Vice-President said the Ayushman Bharat programme has earned global recognition for expanding access to quality healthcare. He noted that nearly 44 crore people have received health insurance coverage of up to ₹5 lakh under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana. Referring to healthcare initiatives for senior citizens, he said free healthcare under the Pradhan Mantri Vaya Vandana Yojana and the ongoing digitisation of health services are making quality healthcare more accessible across the country.

The Vice-President stressed the importance of preventive healthcare and called for concerted efforts to eliminate anaemia among women and children, ensure healthier pregnancies and improve nutrition from infancy through adolescence. He also appealed for greater public awareness about organ and eye donation, describing them as noble acts that save lives and restore hope. 

Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan said the GKNM Group embodies these ideals through its unwavering commitment to healthcare and education, and expressed confidence that the newly inaugurated College of Nursing would produce competent and compassionate healthcare professionals who would contribute significantly to nation-building.

The Vice-President congratulated the trustees, management, faculty, nurses, students and staff of the GKNM Group and wished the institution continued success in its mission of serving society through excellence in healthcare and education. He also expressed hope that the G. Kuppuswamy Naidu Charitable Trust would soon establish a medical college that would produce skilled medical professionals with a spirit of service, committed to caring for the poorest and most vulnerable.

Governor of Tamil Nadu Shri Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar; President, Kuppuswamy Naidu Charity Trust for Education and Medical Relief Shri R. Gopinath; and other dignitaries were present during the occasion

2287760.title: FASTAG BASED TOLL COLLECTION AND DIGITAL TOLLING SYSTEM
2287760.body_html:
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways
FASTAG BASED TOLL COLLECTION AND DIGITAL TOLLING SYSTEM
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 4:59PM by PIB Delhi

The Government has introduced a FASTag based Annual Pass for non-commercial cars, jeeps, and vans, which has come into effect from 15th August, 2025. Under this scheme, an Annual Pass can be activated on payment of Rs. 3,075/- for the year 2026-27 and allows travel through all National Highway/National Expressway fee plazas for one year or up to 200 fee plaza crossings, whichever is earlier. As of June, 2026, more than 77 lakh Annual Passes have been issued registering 63 crore transactions on National Highway Fee Plazas. Presently, around 33% of total Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) transactions done by car/jeep/van are Annual Pass Transactions. The Annual Pass scheme has improved operational efficiency and enhanced the convenience of road users.

The Government through National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has established multiple grievance redressal mechanisms for addressing user fee-related issues on National Highways. Complaints can be lodged through the National Highways 24×7 Toll-Free Helpline 1033, the dedicated email falsededuction@ihmcl.com, the respective FASTag issuer bank helplines, as well as through the RajmargYatra App. These mechanisms are effective, transparent, and easily accessible to road users.

Further, to ensure operational integrity and transparency in user fee collection on National Highways, the Government has implemented FASTag-based electronic toll collection system. Presently, approximately more than 98% of user fee collection takes place through FASTag under National Electronic Toll Collection (NETC) program. All the FASTag transactions are processed in a secure ecosystem involving Toll Management System Software, Acquirer Bank at fee plaza, National Payment Corporation of India (NPCI) as Central Clearing House (CCH) and FASTag Issuer Bank. The transaction involves a transparent process wherein the deducted user fee (Toll) is informed to the highway users and recorded in a central repository. The Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) system is designed as such that no FASTag transaction can take place without the participation of all three stakeholders i.e., Acquirer Bank at user fee plaza, NPCI and Issuer Bank.

The Apex Committee and High-Level Empowered Committee consisting of Experts from Industry and Academia, in view of security and privacy considerations, breach and overall operational control, have recommended further deliberations for GPS-based barrier-free tolling system. However, in an effort to enhance toll operations and enable seamless movement of vehicles, the Government has decided to implement MLFF through Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) with AI analytics and RFID-based Electronic Toll Collection (FASTag) which facilitates barrier-less tolling, where the user fee shall be charged from the vehicle users without having to stop, slow down or stay in a given lane. Multi-Lane Free Flow based barrier less tolling using existing FASTag (RFID)+ANPR/AI- Technology has been awarded on 17 fee plazas as per Annexure A. Out of 17 awarded fee plazas, 05 fee plazas have already gone Live i.e., Choryasi Fee Plaza (Surat, Gujarat); Mundka Fee Plaza (Delhi); Gharaunda Fee Plaza (Haryana); Manoharpura Fee Plaza (Rajasthan); Daulatpura Fee Plaza (Rajasthan). Further, bids have been invited for additional 104 fee plazas as per Annexure B.

2287741.title: NHAI Strengthens Framework for Engaging Professionals in National Highway Consultancy Contracts
2287741.body_html:
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways
NHAI Strengthens Framework for Engaging Professionals in National Highway Consultancy Contracts
Revises Consultancy RFP Provisions to Attract Experienced Engineering Professionals and Young Talent in National Highway Projects
Posted On: 22 JUL 2026 4:41PM by PIB Delhi

With the objective of strengthening technical supervision of National Highway projects, NHAI has made amendments to the Standard Request for Proposal (RFP) documents for deployment of Authority Engineer (AE) and Independent Engineer (IE) consultancy services, mandating minimum remuneration to be paid by the Consultancy Firms to Key Professional, Sub-Professional (Civil Engineer) and Young Professional (Civil Engineer) in future contracts.

Minimum monthly remuneration of Rs. 5.00 Lakhs has been fixed for Team Leader and Bridge/Structural Engineer, Rs. 2.50 Lakhs for Road Safety Expert and Rs. 3.50 Lakhs for Resident cum Highway Engineer, Program Schedule Reviewer, Senior Quality cum Material Expert and Senior Pavement Specialist. In addition to this, minimum monthly remuneration of Rs. 1.50 Lakhs for Sub-Professional (Civil Engineer) and Rs. 1.00 Lakhs for Young Professional (Civil Engineer) has been fixed. Payment of minimum mandated remuneration to the consultancy staff will be ensured through escrow arrangement.

Further to create structured career progression opportunities for experienced Site Engineers, NHAI has revised the policy governing engagement of Site Engineers, which limited their tenure to a maximum of five years. To ensure that these trained professionals continue to contribute to the development of the National Highway network, NHAI has incorporated specific provisions in the General Conditions of Contract (GCC) of the AE/IE consultancy RFPs.

Under the revised framework, a minimum of 20 per cent of the Sub-Professional Engineering Staff deployed by Authority Engineer and Independent Engineer consultancy firms shall comprise previously engaged Site Engineers or Young Professionals from NHAI, MoRTH or NHIDCL. The framework seeks to leverage the experience gained by these professionals in National Highway planning, construction supervision and project management, while simultaneously providing them with meaningful employment opportunities within the Highway infrastructure sector.

To further promote fair and competitive compensation, NHAI has also prescribed that professionals such as Site Engineers and Young Professionals with five years or more of relevant experience shall receive a minimum monthly remuneration of Rs. 1.50 lakhs.

To ensure the deployment of technically qualified, experienced and competent Key Professionals, NHAI has also introduced mandatory empanelment and interview requirements through the NHAI Skill Bridge portal. These provisions have been incorporated into the Consultancy Contract Agreements to strengthen the selection process and enhance the quality of professional engagement in National Highway consultancy assignments.

These reforms represent a significant step towards institutionalizing a sustainable career pathway for engineering professionals associated with National Highway development. The revised provisions will also strengthen technical capabilities of consultancy firms engaged in National Highway development by ensuring greater participation of professionals with hands-on experience in execution and supervision of National Highway projects. This, in turn, will contribute to improved project delivery, enhanced quality standards and greater operational efficiency across the National Highway framework.

By creating opportunities for experienced field engineers to transition into consultancy roles, NHAI seeks to preserve valuable technical knowledge within the sector while enhancing the quality and continuity of project supervision. NHAI remains committed to adopt progressive policy measures that promote professional excellence, attract & retain high-quality engineering talent and build institutional capacity for developing a world-class National Highway network.
